title: Turnover Recognition Reset
primarySkill: Recognising a change of possession.
objective: Develop players’ ability to immediately recognise whether their team has gained or lost possession and adopt the correct attacking or defensive position without waiting for further instruction.
groundSize: 30 metres long × 25 metres wide, divided into one central possession area and four outside positioning gates.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge with one main teaching point
setup:
Mark a central 20-metre × 20-metre possession area.
Place two wide attacking gates outside the left and right edges of the area.
Place two narrow defensive gates closer to the corridor.
Divide players into two evenly numbered teams.
One team begins with the football while the other team shadows without applying contact.
The coach stands outside the area with spare footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The team in possession moves the football by kick or handball inside the central area.
Players without possession maintain light shadow pressure but cannot intercept initially.
The coach calls “turnover” and either gives the football to the other team or rolls a new football into the area.
Players must immediately call either “ours” or “theirs” according to the new possession state.
The team gaining possession spreads towards the two wide attacking gates.
The team losing possession compresses towards the two central defensive gates.
Players hold their new structure for three seconds before play resumes.
After several repetitions, allow defenders to intercept naturally so the turnover cue becomes less predictable.
Rotate the starting team after each one-minute block.
coachingPoints: Players must identify possession change before beginning their movement.
Encourage loud, early communication from more than one player.
The team gaining possession should create width and depth rather than crowding the football.
The team losing possession should protect the corridor before chasing outside.
Players nearest the football should respond differently from players positioned further away.
Avoid all players reacting directly towards the football.
Players should scan before the turnover so their first movement is informed.
Reinforce immediate role change without disappointment, hesitation or argument.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players recognise the change of possession immediately.
Whether communication occurs before movement.
Whether attacking players create usable width and depth.
Whether defensive players compress towards dangerous central space.
Whether players continue performing their previous role after possession changes.
Whether the nearest players and furthest players adopt appropriate different responses.

commonErrors.error: Players continue moving as though their team still has possession.
commonErrors.correction: Stop the repetition and require players to call “ours” or “theirs” before moving.

commonErrors.error: Every player runs directly towards the football.
commonErrors.correction: Assign outside players responsibility for width and inside players responsibility for corridor protection.

commonErrors.error: Players react only after the coach gives a second instruction.
commonErrors.correction: Remove the second instruction and reward the first team that reorganises independently.

commonErrors.error: Communication comes after the movement has already started.
commonErrors.correction: Require the possession call to be made immediately when the football changes teams.

commonErrors.error: Players walk into their transition positions.
commonErrors.correction: Set a three-second movement target while keeping the drill non-contact.

progressions: Allow defenders to intercept passes naturally rather than relying on the coach’s turnover call.
Add a three-second scoring bonus when the attacking team reaches a wide gate quickly.
Add a central scoring gate that the defending team must protect.
Increase the number of players and enlarge the area.
Allow full live play for 15-second periods after each turnover.
regressions: Use only four players per team.
Walk players through the attacking and defensive shapes before beginning.
Use a whistle and clear visual signal for each possession change.
Remove the football and practise the movements as a recognition exercise.
Give each player a fixed attacking and defensive starting position.
successIndicators: Change direction within one second of the turnover.
Protect central space before chasing wide.
Perform the transition response without waiting for the coach.
matchApplication: Australian football regularly changes from attack to defence or defence to attack without a stoppage. Players who recognise the turnover quickly can create an immediate numerical advantage, close dangerous space, provide an outlet or prevent the opposition from using the corridor.

title: Three-Second Transition Response
primarySkill: Executing the correct action during the first three seconds after a turnover.
objective: Develop fast and purposeful player actions during the first three seconds after possession changes, with the new attacking team creating options and the new defending team applying pressure and protecting dangerous space.
groundSize: 35 metres long × 30 metres wide with a scoring gate at each end.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Create a rectangular playing area with a five-metre scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams of four to seven.
Place one target player behind each scoring gate if numbers permit.
The coach begins with several spare footballs on the boundary.
Teams score by moving the football through their attacking gate under control.
Begin with touch pressure before progressing to legal tackling.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team begins in possession and attempts to move the football through its scoring gate.
When a turnover occurs, the coach immediately begins a loud three-second count.
During those three seconds, the team gaining possession must spread, provide a forward option and support the ball carrier.
The team losing possession must pressure the ball carrier, close the nearest short option and recover towards the corridor.
The new attacking team receives two points if it completes a forward disposal or reaches its scoring gate within the three-second window.
The new defending team receives one point if it forces a backwards disposal, stoppage or immediate turnover within three seconds.
If neither team achieves its transition objective, play continues normally for up to 20 seconds.
The coach introduces a new football when the ball leaves the area or play becomes static.
Rotate target players every two minutes.
coachingPoints: The first action after the turnover must be decisive rather than reactive.
The nearest defender applies pressure while teammates protect likely outlets.
The new ball carrier should scan forward before automatically moving sideways or backwards.
Attacking teammates must separate quickly and create different options.
Players behind the football should provide security rather than running past the contest unnecessarily.
Communication should identify pressure, free players and dangerous space.
The three-second rule should create urgency without causing rushed disposal.
Players must continue working after the initial three-second phase.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
The speed of the first reaction after possession changes.
Whether the nearest defender pressures the ball carrier.
Whether additional defenders guard likely handball and kick options.
Whether attacking players create separation instead of crowding.
Whether the ball carrier scans before disposing.
Whether players maintain structure after the three-second count finishes.
Whether urgency improves or simply creates rushed skill execution.

commonErrors.error: The team losing possession appeals, stops or shows disappointment.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce that the next action begins immediately and score defensive transition effort.

commonErrors.error: Several defenders chase the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Nominate the nearest player as pressure and direct others to cover exits.

commonErrors.error: Attacking players run into the same area.
commonErrors.correction: Require one wide option, one forward option and one support option behind the football.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier disposes immediately without scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage one quick scan before committing to the first option.

commonErrors.error: Players stop once the three-second count ends.
commonErrors.correction: Continue play and score the complete transition phase, not only the first reaction.

progressions: Introduce full legal tackling.
Reduce the playing area to increase pressure.
Award additional points for a score created directly from a turnover.
Limit the attacking team to one backwards disposal after regaining possession.
Require the defending team to recover two players into the corridor within three seconds.
Add neutral players who support whichever team has possession.
regressions: Increase the area to provide more decision time.
Stop play immediately after each turnover and rehearse positions.
Extend the transition window from three seconds to five seconds.
Use a coach-directed turnover instead of live interception.
successIndicators: React within one second of a possession change.
Establish pressure on the ball carrier.
Create at least two attacking options.
Protect the corridor after losing possession.
Complete composed disposals despite the urgency constraint.
Continue transitioning after the initial three seconds.
matchApplication: The first three seconds after a turnover often determine whether a team can counterattack into open space or whether the opposition can stabilise defensively. Fast recognition and coordinated first actions reduce easy scores conceded and improve the chance of scoring before defensive structures reset.

title: Attack-to-Defence Recovery
primarySkill: Recovering defensively after losing possession in attack.
objective: Develop the ability to recover from an attacking position into an organised defensive shape immediately after possession is lost.
groundSize: 50 metres long × 35 metres wide with an attacking scoring zone, a central recovery line and a counterattack scoring gate.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark an attacking scoring zone at one end of the area.
Mark a counterattack gate at the opposite end.
Place a recovery line approximately 15 metres behind the attacking scoring zone.
Divide players into an attacking team and a defending team.
Begin with the attacking team positioned ahead of the recovery line.
Position the defending team compactly near the scoring zone.
The coach stands near the attacking end with spare footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession and attempts to enter the scoring zone.
The defending team applies controlled pressure and attempts to intercept or win the football.
When the defending team gains possession, it immediately counterattacks towards the opposite scoring gate.
The player nearest the turnover applies pressure to delay the counterattack.
Other former attacking players sprint goal-side and recover through or towards the central recovery line.
Recovering players must protect the corridor before defending wider options.
The counterattacking team scores two points for reaching the opposite gate and one point for carrying or disposing through the recovery line.
The recovering team scores one point for forcing the football wide and two points for regaining possession before the opposition reaches the gate.
Reset after a score, turnover, boundary exit or 30 seconds of play.
Swap attacking and defending roles after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: The nearest player should pressure and delay rather than attempting an unrealistic immediate tackle.
Players further from the football must recover goal-side at speed.
Recovery runs should be directed towards dangerous space, not simply towards an opponent.
Protect the corridor before defending lower-risk boundary space.
Players should communicate who is pressuring, covering and protecting the deepest option.
Defenders must avoid running past the ball carrier and opening a central lane.
Once the counterattack is slowed, the defensive group should balance and match opponents.
Transition running should continue until the defence is organised, not only until players cross the recovery line.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the nearest player delays the counterattack.
The direction and speed of recovery runs.
Whether players protect central space.
Whether recovering players identify the most dangerous opponent.
Whether communication establishes clear defensive roles.
Whether players stop running once they reach the recovery line.
Whether the team can convert frantic recovery into an organised defensive shape.

commonErrors.error: Players chase the football from behind.
commonErrors.correction: Direct off-ball players to recover goal-side and protect the corridor.

commonErrors.error: The nearest player dives in and is evaded.
commonErrors.correction: Coach the player to close space under control and delay the disposal.

commonErrors.error: Recovering players run towards wide opponents first.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise central space and the deepest dangerous option.

commonErrors.error: Players jog after losing possession.
commonErrors.correction: Score transition effort and rotate players who repeatedly fail to recover.

commonErrors.error: Defenders recover to the same line with no depth.
commonErrors.correction: Establish pressure, cover and deeper balance roles.

progressions: Introduce full tackling.
Add an extra counterattacking player to create numerical disadvantage.
Begin the attacking team deeper inside the scoring zone.
Allow the counterattacking team only eight seconds to score.
Require the recovering team to win possession and immediately counterattack back.
Increase the field width to create more difficult defensive decisions.
regressions: Give the recovering team a numerical advantage.
Require the counterattacking team to complete one sideways disposal before advancing.
Use touch pressure rather than tackling.
Reduce the required recovery distance for Over 35 players or returning players.
successIndicators: Protect the corridor before wide space.
Communicate dangerous opponents and open space.
Prevent direct, uncontested counterattack through the centre.
matchApplication: When a team turns the football over during an attacking phase, many players may be positioned ahead of the ball. Effective attack-to-defence transition requires immediate pressure and purposeful recovery to prevent the opposition from counterattacking through an exposed corridor.

title: Defence-to-Attack Spread
primarySkill: Spreading into attacking positions after regaining possession.
objective: Develop an immediate and coordinated attacking spread after a defensive regain so the ball carrier has safe, progressive and clearly separated disposal options.
groundSize: 40 metres long × 35 metres wide with four outlet gates positioned outside a compact defensive zone.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a compact 20-metre × 20-metre defensive zone in the centre of the area.
Position two wide outlet gates on each side of the area.
Position one forward gate and one deeper safety gate.
Divide players into a defending team and an attacking pressure team.
The defending team begins compactly inside the central zone.
The pressure team begins around the outside and sends the football into the zone.
The coach stands outside the area with spare footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The pressure team kicks or handballs the football into the central defensive zone.
The defending team attempts to intercept, mark, spoil to advantage or win the ground ball.
Once possession is secured, the defending team immediately becomes the attacking team.
The first player outside the contest provides width on the nearest side.
A second player creates an option on the opposite side.
One player pushes forward while another remains behind the football as a safety option.
The team must exit through one of the four outlet gates while retaining possession.
Two points are awarded for using a forward or opposite-side outlet and one point for using the nearest safe outlet.
The opposition applies controlled pressure and attempts to lock the football inside the central zone.
Reset when the football exits through a gate, is turned over or leaves the playing area.
coachingPoints: The first attacking movement should create separation from the contest.
Players should spread to different lanes rather than following the same path.
The player winning possession must be supported from the front, side and behind.
Width should be created before the opposition can establish a press.
The ball carrier should use the safest progressive option, not automatically the nearest teammate.
Opposite-side players must remain engaged and available for a switch.
Players should avoid all running forward and leaving no support behind the football.
Communication should identify wide, forward and safety options.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
How quickly players leave the compact defensive shape.
Whether players create width on both sides.
Whether forward and safety options are available.
Whether players crowd the first possession.
Whether the ball carrier scans the full field.
Whether the team selects a safe but progressive exit.
Whether the opposite side remains available for a switch.

commonErrors.error: Players remain in a defensive cluster after winning possession.
commonErrors.correction: Use outlet gates to give each player a clear spreading responsibility.

commonErrors.error: All players run forward.
commonErrors.correction: Require one designated safety player to remain behind the football.

commonErrors.error: Players spread to the same side.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate near-side, far-side, forward and rear support roles.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier uses the closest option without scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Require a visible head turn before disposal.

commonErrors.error: Wide players move too early and become disconnected.
commonErrors.correction: Time the spread to occur as possession is being secured.

progressions: Allow full pressure after possession is won.
Add a second disposal requirement before the team can exit.
Award extra points for switching to the opposite side.
Reduce the width of the outlet gates.
Add a recovering defender outside the central zone.
Continue play into a second attacking phase after the exit.
regressions: Remove opposition pressure after the regain.
Nominate the required exit before the repetition.
Allow the coach to pause play and reposition players.
Use handball only for younger players.
successIndicators: Spread within two seconds of the regain.
Create width on both sides of the contest.
Exit without crowding the ball carrier.
Retain possession through the first exit.
matchApplication: After an intercept mark, spoil recovery or ground-ball win in defence, players must quickly expand from a compact defensive shape into an attacking shape. Effective spread creates exit options before the opposition can establish repeat pressure.
relatedDrills: TR-009 – First Exit After Defensive Regain

title: Nearest-Player Pressure
primarySkill: Applying immediate pressure through the player nearest the turnover.
objective: Teach the nearest player to apply immediate controlled pressure after possession is lost while teammates close likely attacking options and protect dangerous space.
groundSize: 30 metres long × 25 metres wide with scoring gates at each end.
equipment: Tackle bags for optional technical rehearsal
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a rectangular playing area with a scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams.
Begin with four to seven players per team inside the area.
The coach starts each repetition by giving possession to one team.
Players match up loosely but are not assigned permanent opponents.
Begin with touch pressure before progressing to controlled tackling.
howTheDrillWorks:
The team in possession attempts to move the football through its scoring gate.
When a turnover occurs, the player nearest the new ball carrier must immediately apply pressure.
The second-nearest defender closes the short handball outlet.
The third-nearest defender protects the forward kicking lane or corridor.
Remaining defenders recover goal-side and balance the defensive shape.
The nearest player scores one defensive point by applying effective pressure within two seconds.
The defending team scores an additional point for forcing a backwards disposal, boundary disposal or turnover.
The attacking team scores two points for breaking the first line of pressure and reaching its gate.
The repetition continues for up to 25 seconds.
Reset after a score, turnover, stoppage or boundary exit.
coachingPoints: The nearest player must respond immediately rather than waiting for a teammate.
Close space quickly but reduce speed before contact.
Pressure should remove time and preferred disposal direction.
The nearest player should avoid running past the ball carrier.
Supporting defenders must protect outlets instead of joining the tackle unnecessarily.
Communicate “mine”, “handball”, “corridor” and “deep”.
Apply legal tackling technique with control and appropriate body position.
Pressure remains successful even when it delays or redirects disposal without winning possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the nearest player accepts responsibility immediately.
The speed and control of the pressure approach.
Whether the defender removes the corridor-side option.
Whether second and third defenders cover likely outlets.
Whether multiple players unnecessarily commit to the same contest.
Whether pressure forces a rushed, backwards or wide disposal.
Whether tackling remains legal and controlled.

commonErrors.error: The nearest player waits for another defender.
commonErrors.correction: Stop play and identify nearest-player responsibility at the moment of turnover.

commonErrors.error: The defender approaches too quickly and is sidestepped.
commonErrors.correction: Coach fast closing speed followed by balanced short steps.

commonErrors.error: Two or three defenders tackle the same player.
commonErrors.correction: Assign second and third defenders to outlet and corridor roles.

commonErrors.error: The defender allows an easy inside disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Approach from outside-in and protect the corridor shoulder.

commonErrors.error: Players judge pressure only by whether a tackle is completed.
commonErrors.correction: Reward delays, forced backwards disposals and poor opposition kicks.

progressions: Introduce full legal tackling.
Reduce the size of the area.
Give the attacking team a numerical advantage.
Award three points for a holding-the-ball decision or immediate regain.
Add a second football to create repeated recognition demands.
Continue into a counterattack when the defending team regains possession.
regressions: Freeze play at each turnover and identify the nearest three defenders.
Begin with a coach-directed possession change.
Use three attackers against four defenders.
Remove scoring and focus only on positioning.
successIndicators: Receive support from second and third defenders.
Force rushed, backwards or wide opposition disposal.
matchApplication: Immediate pressure after a turnover prevents an opponent from lifting their eyes and using open space. The nearest player’s action gives teammates time to recover, close options and rebuild defensive structure.

title: Corridor Recovery
primarySkill: Recovering into the corridor after losing possession.
objective: Develop the habit of protecting the corridor and the most dangerous central space before defending lower-risk wide areas after a turnover.
groundSize: 55 metres long × 40 metres wide, divided into left wing, corridor and right wing lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the field lengthways into three lanes.
Make the corridor approximately 15 metres wide.
Place a scoring gate at each end of the corridor.
Divide players into two teams of five to nine.
Begin one team in possession on a wing.
Position the opposition across the field in a balanced shape.
The coach keeps spare footballs near the centre.
howTheDrillWorks:
The team in possession attempts to advance and score through its attacking gate.
Play begins on one wing to create an initially stretched field shape.
When possession changes, the nearest former attacker pressures the ball carrier.
All other former attackers must recover towards the corridor before matching wide opponents.
The new attacking team attempts to use the corridor and score through the opposite gate.
The attacking team receives three points for a controlled corridor score and one point for a wide score.
The defending team receives one point if three players recover into the corridor before the opposition’s second disposal.
The defending team receives two points for forcing the attack outside the corridor and three points for regaining possession.
Continue for up to 35 seconds before resetting.
Restart from alternating wings.
coachingPoints: The corridor is the highest-priority space after a turnover.
The nearest player applies pressure while others recover centrally.
Recovery runs should be angled towards goal-side central positions.
Players should avoid following their direct opponent into harmless wide space.
Defenders must scan both the football and dangerous central runners.
Once the corridor is protected, players can expand to pressure wider options.
Communication should identify the deepest player and unprotected central space.
Defensive recovery must preserve depth rather than forming one flat line.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players instinctively recover centrally.
Whether the nearest player delays the ball carrier.
The angle of recovery runs.
Whether defenders protect depth as well as width.
Whether players become distracted by wide opponents.
Whether central passing lanes are closed before the second opposition disposal.
Whether the defence can later expand without losing its central protection.

commonErrors.error: Players chase their previous opponent towards the boundary.
commonErrors.correction: Direct players to protect dangerous space before reconnecting with opponents.

commonErrors.error: Everyone collapses directly onto the football.
commonErrors.correction: Keep deeper defenders in corridor-cover positions.

commonErrors.error: Recovery runs are straight backwards with no reference to the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Use coloured corridor markers as movement targets.

commonErrors.error: The nearest player also sprints back and gives the ball carrier time.
commonErrors.correction: Assign the nearest player to delay while teammates recover.

commonErrors.error: Defenders form one flat line.
commonErrors.correction: Require pressure, cover and deeper balance.

progressions: Remove the lane cones once the recovery habit is established.
Give the new attacking team an extra player.
Allow full tackling.
Add a second scoring gate outside the corridor.
Require the defending team to counterattack after regaining possession.
Start from a deeper attacking position with more players ahead of the football.
regressions: Pause after each turnover and check positions.
Give the recovering team a numerical advantage.
Use jogging pace for the first teaching repetitions.
successIndicators: Delay the ball carrier through nearest-player pressure.
Force the opposition towards wider, lower-value areas.
Reorganise before the opposition’s second or third disposal.
matchApplication: Corridor turnovers frequently lead to fast scoring opportunities because they provide the shortest route to goal. Recovering centrally after losing possession reduces the opposition’s ability to attack through the most dangerous part of the ground.
relatedDrills: TR-009 – First Exit After Defensive Regain

title: First Possession Security
primarySkill: Securing and retaining the first possession after a turnover opportunity.
objective: Develop the ability to win the first possession after a turnover opportunity and complete a secure first disposal before attempting to expand or attack aggressively.
groundSize: 25 metres long × 25 metres wide with four outside release gates.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a 20-metre × 20-metre contest square.
Position one release gate outside each side of the square.
Divide players into two teams of four to seven.
Begin players evenly distributed around the square.
The coach stands on the boundary with several footballs.
Nominate one support player from each team who begins outside the square.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach rolls, bounces or kicks a football into the contest square.
Both teams compete to win the first possession.
The player winning possession must protect the football and identify a secure first disposal.
Teammates provide one close release option and one outside spreading option.
The team cannot score by exiting immediately from a rushed possession.
One point is awarded for winning the first possession.
A second point is awarded for completing the first disposal to a teammate.
A third point is awarded for retaining possession and exiting through a release gate.
If the first disposal is turned over, the other team can immediately score using the same sequence.
Rotate outside support players every two repetitions.
coachingPoints: The first priority is clean possession, not immediate distance.
Players should lower their body, protect the football and keep their feet where possible.
The first support player should provide a clear, short release.
Other teammates should spread once possession is secure.
The ball carrier must distinguish between genuine pressure and perceived pressure.
Avoid blind handballs or kicks away from the contest.
Communicate before the player takes possession.
After the first disposal, players must continue supporting the transition.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Body position when collecting the football.
Whether players protect possession under contact.
Whether support is available before the ball is won.
The quality and direction of the first disposal.
Whether players rush to exit before possession is stable.
Whether teammates spread after the secure release.
Whether the team retains possession beyond the first action.

commonErrors.error: Players attempt to kick the football forward before controlling it.
commonErrors.correction: Require possession and a secure disposal before an exit can score.

commonErrors.error: The ball winner stands upright in contact.
commonErrors.correction: Coach lower hips, strong body position and football protection.

commonErrors.error: Teammates crowd the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Assign one close release and others to outside gates.

commonErrors.error: The first handball is blind.
commonErrors.correction: Require the receiver to communicate before the ball winner disposes.

commonErrors.error: Players relax after completing the first disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Continue scoring through the release gate to reinforce the full transition phase.

progressions: Increase contact to match-like legal pressure.
Reduce the size of the contest square.
Remove the nominated outside support players.
Require the exit to occur through a gate nominated after possession is won.
Add a five-second limit to secure the first disposal.
Continue into a larger transition area after the exit.
regressions: Place a stationary support player behind the contest.
Allow the coach to nominate the first disposal.
Roll the football predictably to one side.
successIndicators: Win or halve the initial contest.
Retain possession through the second action.
Spread only after the football is secured.
matchApplication: Many transition opportunities begin with an intercept, loose football, spoil or disputed possession. Teams cannot counterattack effectively unless the first possession and first disposal are secure. Clean control allows the team to expand without immediately returning the football to the opposition.

title: Support Run Connection
primarySkill: Providing connected support runs after possession is regained.
objective: Develop coordinated support running that provides the ball carrier with forward, lateral and trailing options during defence-to-attack transition.
groundSize: 50 metres long × 35 metres wide with three horizontal transition zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the area into defensive, middle and attacking transition zones.
Place a scoring gate at the far end.
Divide players into two teams of five to eight.
Begin the defending team compactly in the defensive zone.
Begin the attacking pressure team around them.
Position the coach near the defensive zone with spare footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The pressure team sends the football into the defensive zone.
The defending team attempts to regain possession.
Once possession is secured, the team transitions towards the scoring gate.
The first support runner provides a lateral or angled outlet.
A second runner pushes ahead of the football into the next zone.
A third runner remains behind the football as a trailing safety option.
Players must maintain connection so the ball carrier is not isolated.
The team scores one point for entering the middle zone, one point for entering the attacking zone and two points for scoring through the gate.
A bonus point is awarded if at least three different support roles contribute to the transition.
If the opposition regains possession, roles immediately reverse.
coachingPoints: Support runners should create different angles, distances and depths.
The first support option must arrive early enough to assist the regain.
Forward runners should not leave before possession is secure.
Trailing support protects against a missed skill or backwards pressure.
Players should run to useful space rather than simply running past the ball carrier.
Disposal timing should allow runners to receive at speed.
The ball carrier should avoid holding the football until all options are covered.
Players must continue supporting after giving a disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether support exists at multiple depths.
The timing of forward runs.
Whether players provide useful angles.
Whether the ball carrier becomes isolated.
Whether players continue running after disposal.
Whether trailing support remains available.
Whether the team maintains connection across all three zones.

commonErrors.error: Every support runner moves ahead of the football.
commonErrors.correction: Assign a trailing safety role behind the ball carrier.

commonErrors.error: Players run directly beside each other.
commonErrors.correction: Require different widths, angles and depths.

commonErrors.error: Forward runners leave before possession is secured.
commonErrors.correction: Delay the forward run until the ball winner has control.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after disposing.
commonErrors.correction: Require give-and-go movement into the next support position.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier holds the football too long.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage early disposal to a runner moving into space.

progressions: Add full live pressure.
Reduce the width of the area.
Require one switch of play during the transition.
Add a recovering defender entering from behind.
Limit the number of disposals allowed in each zone.
Continue play back in the opposite direction after a turnover.
regressions: Remove opposition pressure after the regain.
Allow one extra player for the transitioning team.
Increase the width of each zone.
Walk through the support roles before live play.
Shorten the running distance for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Provide support ahead, beside and behind the football.
Time forward runs after possession is secured.
Move the football through all zones without isolating the ball carrier.
matchApplication: Successful counterattack depends on more than the first ball winner. Players must run into connected positions that allow the football to move away from pressure and through open space before the opposition recovers.

title: First Exit After Defensive Regain
primarySkill: Selecting and executing the first exit after regaining possession in defence.
objective: Develop composed decision making and coordinated outlet movement for the first disposal and exit after a defensive regain.
groundSize: Defensive half of an oval or an area approximately 65 metres long × 50 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Use the defensive half of the ground.
Position a defending team inside defensive 50.
Position an attacking team across forward 50 and the high half-forward area.
Mark three exit routes: boundary outlet, central release and opposite-side switch.
Place a target gate beyond defensive 50.
Begin each repetition with an opposition forward entry from outside the area.
The coach holds spare footballs near the attacking side.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team sends the football inside 50 and attempts to score.
The defending team attempts to intercept, spoil to advantage or win the ground ball.
Once possession is secured, defenders immediately spread into outlet positions.
The ball winner scans the boundary outlet, central release, opposite-side switch and safe support behind the football.
The team attempts to complete its first disposal and exit beyond defensive 50 while retaining possession.
One point is awarded for securing the regain.
One point is awarded for completing the first disposal.
Two points are awarded for exiting beyond defensive 50.
A bonus point is awarded for using the opposite side when the near side is blocked.
The attacking team receives two points for forcing a repeat entry and three points for scoring after the turnover.
Reset after a successful exit, score, stoppage or second turnover.
Rotate positional groups after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Secure the football before attempting the exit.
The first disposal should reduce pressure rather than transfer pressure to a teammate.
Defenders without possession must create width immediately.
The deepest defender may provide a safe switch or reset option.
The corridor should be used when genuinely open, not forced.
Boundary exits are acceptable when they move the football away from immediate danger.
The ball carrier should scan both sides before committing.
Players must continue supporting after the first disposal to complete the exit.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
How the defensive regain is secured.
Whether outlet players spread before the ball winner is trapped.
Whether the ball carrier scans multiple options.
The pressure level placed on the intended receiver.
Whether players recognise when to switch.
Whether the first disposal contributes to an actual exit.
Whether the team remains connected beyond defensive 50.
Whether turnovers occur centrally or in lower-risk wide areas.

commonErrors.error: The ball winner disposes immediately to a covered teammate.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage a quick scan and use of the safest progressive option.

commonErrors.error: Outlet players remain close to the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Assign width responsibilities to half-backs, wings and deeper defenders.

commonErrors.error: The team forces the corridor when it is closed.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce that corridor use depends on pressure and available support.

commonErrors.error: The first disposal is completed but the receiver has no next option.
commonErrors.correction: Build second and third support movements into the exit pattern.

commonErrors.error: Players repeatedly exit to the same side.
commonErrors.correction: Reward recognition and use of the opposite-side switch.

progressions: Allow full match-like pressure.
Add opposition players behind the defensive 50 exit line.
Continue play to an inside-50 entry at the opposite end.
Begin with varied entries including high balls, ground balls and shallow entries.
Add a time limit for the first exit.
Remove the marked exit routes and require players to recognise them naturally.
regressions: Use six defenders against four attackers.
Allow the defence to secure the mark before pressure begins.
Shorten the distance to the exit gate.
Begin with a controlled intercept mark.
successIndicators: Recognise when to use a switch.
Exit beyond defensive 50 while retaining possession.
matchApplication: The first exit after a defensive regain often determines whether a team escapes pressure or concedes a repeat entry. A composed first disposal, supported by width and clear outlets, allows the team to transition from defence into attack.

title: Transition Fundamentals Assessment
primarySkill: Integrating fundamental attack-to-defence and defence-to-attack transition behaviours.
objective: Assess whether players can recognise and execute the appropriate fundamental transition behaviours during continuous, realistic changes of possession.
groundSize: 70 metres long × 50 metres wide with scoring zones at each end and a marked central corridor.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a rectangular field with a scoring zone at each end.
Mark a central corridor approximately 18 metres wide.
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Position players across defensive, midfield and attacking lines.
The coach stands centrally with several spare footballs.
Appoint assistant coaches or injured players as transition observers if available.
Prepare an assessment sheet containing the following categories:
Turnover recognition
First-three-second response
Nearest-player pressure
Corridor recovery
First-possession security
Attacking spread
Support running
First exit
howTheDrillWorks:
One team begins in possession and attempts to move the football into its scoring zone.
Play remains continuous when possession changes.
The team gaining possession must secure the first possession, spread and provide connected support.
The team losing possession must apply nearest-player pressure, recover towards the corridor and organise behind the football.
Teams receive one point for entering their scoring zone and two points for completing a score.
A transition bonus point is awarded when a team demonstrates at least three correct transition behaviours during the same phase.
The coach may introduce a new football to create a sudden possession change when play becomes slow or predictable.
Play four blocks of four minutes with one minute of feedback between blocks.
Coaches assess each team and selected individual players during every block.
After the final block, players complete one unrestricted period without transition bonus scoring.
The coach compares behaviour during the scored and unrestricted periods.
Finish with brief individual and team feedback based on observed actions.
coachingPoints: Recognition of the turnover must occur before tactical movement.
The nearest player applies pressure while others protect space.
Defensive recovery should prioritise the corridor and goal-side positioning.
The team gaining possession must secure the football before expanding.
Attacking players should create width, depth and connected support.
The first disposal should reduce pressure and begin the transition.
Players must continue their transition work beyond the first action.
Communication should identify possession state, pressure, outlets and dangerous space.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
How quickly players recognise possession change.
Whether the nearest player applies effective pressure.
Whether defenders recover centrally and goal-side.
Whether the first possession is secured.
Whether the first disposal reduces pressure.
Whether attacking players create width and depth.
Whether support runners remain connected.
Whether players maintain transition effort after the first disposal.
Whether the same players repeatedly fail to react.
Whether behaviours transfer into unrestricted play.

commonErrors.error: Players react only when the coach calls the turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Allow continuous play and assess independent recognition.

commonErrors.error: The entire defensive group chases the football.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce nearest-player pressure with corridor recovery behind it.

commonErrors.error: The team gaining possession spreads before controlling the football.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise first-possession security and a clear release.

commonErrors.error: Support runners become disconnected from the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Require front, lateral and trailing support at usable distances.

commonErrors.error: Players perform correctly only when bonus points are available.
commonErrors.correction: Include an unrestricted final block and compare the behaviours.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after the first transition action.
commonErrors.correction: Assess the complete phase until structure is established.

progressions: Increase the playing area to full-ground transition.
Allow full match-like contact.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Create numerical imbalance after selected turnovers.
Require a score within 15 seconds of a regain.
Add positional transition responsibilities for defenders, midfielders, wings and forwards.
Use video recording for post-session review.
regressions: Pause after turnovers to review positioning.
Assess only three transition behaviours at a time.
Give one team a numerical advantage.
Use shorter playing blocks for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Apply pressure through the nearest player.
Recover into the corridor after losing possession.
Secure the first possession after a regain.
Exit pressure and establish a new attacking structure.
Maintain the behaviours during unrestricted play.
matchApplication: This drill combines the fundamental transition actions required during match play. It assesses whether players can move from attack to defence and defence to attack without relying on stoppages, coach direction or predetermined movement patterns.
relatedDrills: TR-009 – First Exit After Defensive Regain

title: Transition Voice Commands
primarySkill: Using immediate communication to organise transition roles.
objective: Develop clear, early and specific communication that helps teammates recognise possession change and organise their first transition actions.
groundSize: 30 metres long × 25 metres wide with a central playing zone and two scoring gates.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge with one main teaching point
setup:
Mark a rectangular playing area with one scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two evenly numbered teams.
Position four coloured role markers outside the area representing pressure, cover, width and support.
Begin with one team moving the football under low pressure.
Nominate one player from each team as the initial transition caller.
Place spare footballs with the coach on the boundary.
howTheDrillWorks:
The team in possession moves the football by handball and short kick.
The coach creates a turnover by calling a team colour and feeding a new football to that team.
The nominated caller must immediately call “ours” or “theirs”.
The caller then gives one specific instruction such as “pressure”, “corridor”, “wide” or “support”.
Teammates respond to the call and move into the appropriate transition roles.
The new attacking team attempts to score through its gate.
The new defending team attempts to delay and protect the corridor.
A team receives one point for an immediate possession call and one point for a correct role instruction.
Change the nominated caller after every two turnovers.
Progress to live interceptions once communication becomes consistent.
coachingPoints: Communication must occur at the moment possession changes.
Calls should identify an action rather than simply create noise.
More than one player may communicate, but calls must not conflict.
Players furthest from the football often have the clearest view.
Defensive calls should identify pressure, corridor and deepest danger.
Attacking calls should identify width, forward options and support behind.
Players must act on the communication rather than only repeating it.
Leadership responsibility should rotate through the entire group.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether possession change is called immediately.
Whether communication is specific and useful.
Whether players respond to the call.
Whether multiple calls support or contradict each other.
Whether quieter players communicate when given responsibility.
Whether players away from the football provide information.
Whether communication continues after the first transition action.

commonErrors.error: Players call only the team name.
commonErrors.correction: Require the second call to identify the required action.

commonErrors.error: Communication occurs after teammates have already moved.
commonErrors.correction: Award points only for calls made within one second of the turnover.

commonErrors.error: Several players shout conflicting instructions.
commonErrors.correction: Establish priority calls: possession state, pressure, corridor, outlet.

commonErrors.error: Only natural leaders communicate.
commonErrors.correction: Rotate the designated caller regularly.

commonErrors.error: Players call correctly but do not move.
commonErrors.correction: Score communication only when the team responds with the correct action.

progressions: Remove the designated caller and require collective communication.
Allow live turnovers through interception.
Add full pressure after the initial call.
Require the defending team to identify the deepest dangerous player.
Require the attacking team to call both a wide and a forward option.
Record communication during a live small-sided game.
regressions: Display the approved calls on marker cards.
Allow the coach to prompt the first word.
successIndicators: Call possession change within one second.
Communicate from both near and far positions.
Maintain useful communication throughout the transition phase.
matchApplication: During a match, players often have different views of the turnover and developing space. Clear communication helps the nearest player pressure, recovering defenders protect dangerous areas and attacking players create outlets before the opposition reorganises.

title: Shape Flip Lanes
primarySkill: Changing between attacking width and defensive compactness.
objective: Teach players to rapidly change team shape by expanding when possession is gained and contracting when possession is lost.
groundSize: 40 metres long × 35 metres wide, divided into two wide lanes and one central lane.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Divide the playing area lengthways into three equal lanes.
Place one scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams of four to eight.
Begin the team in possession with at least one player in each lane.
Begin the defending team inside the central lane and adjacent inside edges.
The coach stands centrally with spare footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team moves the football towards its scoring gate.
At least one attacking player must occupy each lane.
When possession changes, the new defending team must contract towards the central lane.
The new attacking team must expand and occupy all three lanes.
The team gaining possession scores one transition point if it creates three-lane width within three seconds.
The team losing possession scores one transition point if it places at least three players in or beside the central lane within three seconds.
Play continues until a team scores through an end gate or turns the football over.
Players may move between lanes but should avoid unnecessary crowding.
Restart from the opposite end after each score.
Rotate starting positions every two minutes.
coachingPoints: Attacking shape should stretch the opposition horizontally.
Defensive shape should reduce central space.
The turnover must trigger an immediate change in spacing.
Wide players should remain connected and available rather than standing on the boundary.
Defenders should contract without all collapsing directly onto the ball.
Players behind the football should protect central depth.
The nearest player can pressure while others change the overall shape.
Communication should identify “wide”, “inside” and “deep” roles.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
How quickly the team shape changes.
Whether attacking players occupy useful width.
Whether defenders protect the central lane.
Whether players crowd the football during either transition.
Whether width remains connected to the ball carrier.
Whether defensive compactness retains depth.
Whether players recognise their role without coach direction.

commonErrors.error: Players remain in the same shape after a turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Freeze play and compare the required attacking and defensive shapes.

commonErrors.error: Attacking width becomes too disconnected.
commonErrors.correction: Set a maximum distance between the ball carrier and the nearest wide option.

commonErrors.error: Defenders all collapse onto the ball.
commonErrors.correction: Keep one player deeper and one player protecting the next central lane.

commonErrors.error: Wide players enter the central lane too early.
commonErrors.correction: Require three-lane occupation until the first clean disposal is completed.

commonErrors.error: Players move slowly between shapes.
commonErrors.correction: Use a three-second transition score.

progressions: Allow live tackling.
Remove the lane cones.
Reduce the field width.
Add a neutral player supporting the team in possession.
Award extra points for switching from one wide lane to the other.
Continue play after a score into an immediate reverse transition.
successIndicators: Expand into three lanes after gaining possession.
Contract towards central space after losing possession.
matchApplication: AFL teams require width and separation to use the football, but must become compact when defending. The ability to flip shape immediately helps create attacking options while reducing the opposition’s access to dangerous central space.

title: Ball-Side and Far-Side Reaction
primarySkill: Performing different transition roles according to field position.
objective: Develop distinct ball-side and far-side transition responses so players close to the football apply pressure or support while players away from it protect balance and width.
groundSize: 45 metres long × 40 metres wide, divided into ball-side and far-side halves.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the playing area lengthways into two halves.
Mark one scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams.
Begin play with the football on one side of the field.
Position players across both halves.
Identify the side containing the football as ball-side and the opposite side as far-side.
howTheDrillWorks:
The team in possession attempts to move the football towards its scoring gate.
When the football changes teams, players identify whether they are ball-side or far-side.
Ball-side defenders apply pressure and close short disposal options.
Far-side defenders recover towards the corridor and protect deeper space.
Ball-side attackers provide immediate release and overlap.
Far-side attackers maintain width and prepare for a switch.
The attacking team receives two points for using a far-side option after a regain.
The defending team receives one point for closing the ball-side exit and one point for protecting the far-side switch.
Play continues for up to 30 seconds.
Reset with the football starting from alternating sides.
coachingPoints: Transition responsibility depends on location relative to the football.
Ball-side players should act immediately and aggressively.
Far-side players should preserve team balance.
Far-side defenders should not become passive spectators.
Far-side attackers should remain wide enough to stretch the defence.
The corridor must remain protected during far-side movement.
Players should scan across the full field before and after the turnover.
Communication should identify the open or dangerous opposite side.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players identify ball-side and far-side roles.
Whether ball-side defenders pressure quickly.
Whether far-side defenders protect central and deep space.
Whether attacking support is provided near the football.
Whether far-side attacking width remains available.
Whether players overcommit to the ball-side.
Whether the switch is recognised and defended.

commonErrors.error: Far-side defenders run directly to the football.
commonErrors.correction: Hold them in central cover and switch-protection positions.

commonErrors.error: Far-side attackers drift into congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Require them to maintain width until the ball carrier scans.

commonErrors.error: Ball-side defenders guard space without pressuring.
commonErrors.correction: Assign the nearest ball-side player to close the ball carrier.

commonErrors.error: Players fail to adjust when the football switches sides.
commonErrors.correction: Call “new ball-side” and require immediate role reversal.

commonErrors.error: Far-side players stop communicating.
commonErrors.correction: Make far-side players responsible for calling deep and switch threats.

progressions: Remove the halfway line.
Allow full legal tackling.
Add a neutral player on the far side.
Award extra points for a successful switch followed by forward movement.
Add a recovering player entering from behind.
Continue through multiple turnovers without resetting.
regressions: Stop play and identify ball-side and far-side players.
Keep fixed side roles for several repetitions.
successIndicators: Protect corridor and depth on the far side.
Adjust roles when the football changes sides.
matchApplication: Players positioned close to a turnover face different demands from those on the opposite side of the ground. Effective teams combine immediate ball-side action with far-side balance, preventing overcommitment and preserving attacking switch options.

title: Stop the First Forward Disposal
primarySkill: Preventing the opposition’s first forward disposal after a turnover.
objective: Develop coordinated pressure and coverage that prevents the opposition from immediately moving the football forward after regaining possession.
groundSize: 35 metres long × 25 metres wide with a forward scoring gate and a rear safety gate at each end.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a rectangular area.
Place one forward scoring gate and one rear safety gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams of four to seven.
Begin one team in possession in the middle of the area.
Position both teams in a balanced spread.
The coach holds spare footballs on the boundary.
howTheDrillWorks:
The team in possession attempts to reach its forward scoring gate.
When possession changes, the new defending team must stop the first forward disposal.
The nearest defender pressures the ball carrier.
Supporting defenders close the short forward handball and kick lanes.
The new attacking team may use a backwards or sideways disposal to retain possession.
The attacking team receives two points if its first disposal goes forward and reaches a teammate.
The defending team receives one point if it forces the first disposal sideways or backwards.
The defending team receives two points if it forces an immediate turnover or stoppage.
After the first disposal, play continues normally towards the scoring gate.
Reset after a score, boundary exit or 25 seconds.
coachingPoints: The nearest defender must reduce the ball carrier’s time.
Supporting defenders should close forward options rather than all chasing the ball.
Defenders should protect the corridor shoulder.
Forcing a backwards disposal is a successful outcome.
Pressure should remain controlled to avoid being sidestepped.
Defenders must scan the ball carrier and likely receivers.
The team should reorganise behind the initial pressure.
Players must continue defending after the first disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the nearest player pressures within two seconds.
Whether forward handball and kick lanes are covered.
Whether defenders overcommit to the contest.
Whether the opposition is forced sideways or backwards.
Whether the defence builds structure behind the pressure.
Whether defenders continue after the first disposal.
Whether legal contact and tackling technique are maintained.

commonErrors.error: Defenders chase the ball carrier from behind.
commonErrors.correction: Use angle and approach to protect the forward side.

commonErrors.error: Multiple defenders pressure the same player.
commonErrors.correction: Assign supporting defenders to the first forward options.

commonErrors.error: Players treat a sideways disposal as defensive failure.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce that preventing forward movement is the initial goal.

commonErrors.error: The nearest player approaches out of control.
commonErrors.correction: Close quickly, then shorten steps before contact.

commonErrors.error: Defenders stop after forcing one backwards disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Require the team to continue until structure is restored.

progressions: Allow full tackling.
Reduce the playing area.
Give the attacking team an extra player.
Award three points for a first-disposal forward mark.
Continue play for multiple turnovers.
Remove the rear safety gates.
regressions: Give the defending team a numerical advantage.
Require the attacking team to handball first.
successIndicators: Pressure the new ball carrier immediately.
Build defensive shape behind the pressure.
matchApplication: Stopping the first forward disposal after a turnover prevents the opposition from exploiting unstructured space. Even when possession is not regained, forcing the football sideways or backwards gives teammates time to recover and organise.

title: Outlet Separation Triangle
primarySkill: Creating three clearly separated options after regaining possession.
objective: Develop a consistent three-option outlet shape that provides the ball carrier with forward, lateral and safety support after a regain.
groundSize: 30 metres long × 30 metres wide with four turnover starting zones.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge with one main teaching point
setup:
Mark a central contest square approximately 10 metres × 10 metres.
Place three outlet cones around each side of the square: one forward, one lateral and one behind.
Divide players into two teams.
Begin two players from each team inside the square.
Position remaining players around the outside.
The coach stands beside the square with spare footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach feeds the football into the central square.
Players compete under controlled pressure to secure possession.
Once a team wins the football, three teammates move to form a triangle around the ball carrier.
One player provides a forward option.
One player provides a lateral option.
One player provides a safety option behind the football.
The ball carrier scans and selects the most appropriate outlet.
The team receives one point for forming the three-option shape and one point for completing the disposal.
The opposition may shadow the outlets but cannot tackle initially.
Rotate inside and outside players every three repetitions.
coachingPoints: The three options must be separated by angle and distance.
Players should not stand in a straight line.
The forward option should move into space rather than directly away from the ball carrier.
The lateral option should provide a clear release from pressure.
The safety option must remain behind and connected.
The ball carrier should scan all three options.
Support players should communicate before the disposal.
The shape should form as possession is being secured.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether three distinct options are created.
Whether players form useful angles.
Whether the safety option remains available.
Whether the forward option leaves too early.
Whether the ball carrier scans all outlets.
Whether support communication is clear.
Whether the shape forms before pressure arrives.

commonErrors.error: Support players stand on the same line.
commonErrors.correction: Use cones to create three different angles.

commonErrors.error: All options move forward.
commonErrors.correction: Assign one player to remain behind the football.

commonErrors.error: Support forms after the ball carrier is trapped.
commonErrors.correction: Trigger movement as possession is being won.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier automatically uses the closest option.
commonErrors.correction: Require a visible scan of all three outlets.

commonErrors.error: The safety option stands too close.
commonErrors.correction: Set a minimum five-metre separation.

progressions: Allow defenders to intercept outlet disposals.
Add full pressure after possession is secured.
Remove the outlet cones.
Require the ball to reach a second support player.
Add a fourth option on the opposite side.
Continue into a larger transition area.
successIndicators: Form forward, lateral and safety options.
Maintain support after the ball leaves the contest.
matchApplication: After a contested regain, the ball carrier needs more than one predictable option. A well-spaced triangle creates an immediate release, a progressive option and protection against pressure from behind.
relatedDrills: TR-009 – First Exit After Defensive Regain

title: Defensive Fold Behind Pressure
primarySkill: Folding defenders behind the player applying pressure.
objective: Develop coordinated defensive folding so immediate pressure is supported by layers of cover and deeper protection after possession is lost.
groundSize: 50 metres long × 35 metres wide with three defensive fold lines.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark three horizontal lines across the field, approximately 12 metres apart.
Place a scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams.
Begin one team in possession in the middle third.
Position players across all three lines.
The coach stands on the boundary with spare footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to advance through the scoring gate.
When possession changes, the nearest former attacker pressures the new ball carrier.
The second layer folds behind the pressure to cover short and central options.
The deepest layer recovers to protect space behind the defence.
Players may not all defend on the same line.
The defending team receives one point for establishing three defensive layers.
It receives another point for forcing a backwards or wide disposal.
The attacking team receives two points for breaking through all three layers.
Play continues until a score, turnover or 30-second limit.
Reset from alternating field positions.
coachingPoints: The pressure player should delay and direct the ball carrier.
The second layer protects the next disposal.
The deepest layer protects against a kick over the top.
Defenders should fold on angles rather than running straight backwards.
Players must maintain connection between layers.
Communication should identify pressure, cover and deepest responsibility.
The defence should avoid becoming flat.
Once pressure slows the attack, the layers can compress further.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the nearest player pressures immediately.
Whether support folds behind rather than beside the pressure.
Whether a deeper defender remains behind the play.
Whether distances between layers remain connected.
Whether defenders communicate role changes.
Whether the attack is forced sideways or backwards.
Whether the defence becomes flat after multiple disposals.

commonErrors.error: All defenders recover to the same line.
commonErrors.correction: Assign clear pressure, cover and deepest roles.

commonErrors.error: The second layer chases the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Hold it in the likely next-disposal lane.

commonErrors.error: The deepest player moves too close to the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the space behind until the attack is delayed.

commonErrors.error: Gaps between layers become too large.
commonErrors.correction: Set maximum connection distances between lines.

commonErrors.error: Players run directly backwards without scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Use angled recovery while viewing ball and opponent.

progressions: Remove the marked fold lines.
Allow full tackling.
Give the attacking team a numerical advantage.
Start the turnover closer to goal.
Continue play through multiple turnover phases.
Add a counterattack requirement after a defensive regain.
regressions: Give the defending team an extra player.
successIndicators: Force the opposition away from direct attacking space.
matchApplication: Immediate pressure is ineffective if there is no defensive cover behind it. Folding players into connected layers reduces easy forward options, protects against the kick over the top and allows the team to rebuild its defensive structure.
relatedDrills: TR-014 – Stop the First Forward Disposal

title: Transition Relay Chain
primarySkill: Maintaining continuous movement and support through a transition chain.
objective: Develop repeated support and repositioning habits so players remain involved through several consecutive actions after possession changes.
groundSize: 45 metres long × 25 metres wide with four transition stations.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark four stations in a zigzag pattern from one end of the area to the other.
Place two players from each team at or near each station.
Begin with one football at the first station.
Assign one team to attack forward and the other to provide shadow pressure.
The coach stands centrally to call turnover moments.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team moves the football through the four stations.
After disposing, each player continues running to become support at the next station.
Shadow defenders track and apply controlled pressure.
At any point, the coach calls “turnover” and feeds a second football to the shadow team.
Roles reverse immediately.
The former attacking team must recover through the stations in the opposite direction.
Players receive one point for completing all four stations without losing connection.
A second point is awarded when every player who disposes provides a second support action.
Run repetitions for 60–75 seconds before rotating starting positions.
Progress to live interception when movement patterns are established.
coachingPoints: Disposal does not end a player’s involvement.
Players should run to support the next action.
Support angles should change as the football moves.
The turnover requires immediate direction change.
The nearest former attacker pressures while others recover.
Players should communicate the next station and available option.
Running speed should match the ball movement.
Maintain skill quality under repeated movement.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players continue moving after disposal.
Whether support arrives before the ball carrier is isolated.
Whether players react quickly to the turnover call.
Whether running angles remain useful.
Whether skill quality deteriorates under fatigue.
Whether defenders recover with purpose.
Whether every player contributes repeatedly.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after disposing.
commonErrors.correction: Require every disposer to provide the next support action.

commonErrors.error: Support runners follow directly behind each other.
commonErrors.correction: Use angled stations and demand varied running lanes.

commonErrors.error: Players react slowly when roles reverse.
commonErrors.correction: Award points for the first team to reorganise.

commonErrors.error: The football moves faster than support.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce disposal speed or increase running urgency.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue causes poor technique.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten work periods and restore execution quality.

progressions: Allow live interception.
Add full pressure at the final two stations.
Reduce spacing between stations.
Use two footballs simultaneously.
Require a kick at selected stations.
Continue immediately back in the opposite direction after completion.
successIndicators: Complete multiple transition actions without stopping.
matchApplication: Transition rarely ends after one disposal. Players must continue running, supporting and repositioning across several actions as the football moves through the ground or changes teams again.

title: Fast or Secure Decision
primarySkill: Choosing whether to counterattack quickly or secure possession after a regain.
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise when a fast counterattack is available and when possession should be stabilised before advancing.
groundSize: 50 metres long × 40 metres wide with a fast-attack gate and two secure-possession gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark one narrow forward gate at each end.
Mark two wider lateral safety gates near the middle of each side boundary.
Divide players into two teams.
Begin with balanced numbers in the centre.
The coach varies the pressure and available space at each turnover.
Place spare footballs around the boundary.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team begins in possession and attempts to score.
When possession changes, the new ball carrier scans the field.
If the forward gate is open, the team may attack quickly for three points.
If the forward gate is covered, the team may exit through a lateral safety gate for one point.
After using a safety gate, the team retains possession and re-enters through the side.
Defenders attempt to disguise whether the fast option is genuinely available.
A rushed turnover through the forward gate results in two points to the opposition.
The coach varies numerical balance and starting positions.
Play continues for 30-second phases.
Teams briefly explain selected decisions during recovery periods.
coachingPoints: Fast play is appropriate only when space and support are available.
Securing possession is not passive when the direct route is closed.
The ball carrier must scan before deciding.
Teammates should communicate “go” or “hold”.
Forward runners must be genuinely available, not merely moving ahead.
Safety options should reduce pressure and preserve possession.
Avoid predetermined decisions before the turnover occurs.
The next action should match the field picture.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the ball carrier scans forward first.
Whether the team identifies available numbers and space.
Whether players force the fast option.
Whether safety options remain available.
Whether communication supports the decision.
Whether secure possession leads to a later attack.
Whether players can explain their choice.

commonErrors.error: Players always attack forward immediately.
commonErrors.correction: Reward correct use of the safety gate when the forward lane is closed.

commonErrors.error: Players always choose the safe option.
commonErrors.correction: Award greater points for recognising genuine fast opportunities.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier decides before scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Require a visible head turn before disposal.

commonErrors.error: Forward runners call for the football while covered.
commonErrors.correction: Teach runners to assess defender position before calling.

commonErrors.error: Securing possession becomes slow and static.
commonErrors.correction: Require immediate support and re-entry after the safety gate.

progressions: Remove the coloured gates.
Allow full match-like pressure.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Give the defending team delayed recovery players.
Continue to a full score after the first decision.
Require the ball carrier to use a verbal call before disposal.
successIndicators: Maintain possession after securing the football.
Explain the reason for their choice.
matchApplication: Not every regain should produce an immediate counterattack. Good transition teams recognise when the opposition is exposed and when pressure requires a secure first phase before attacking.
relatedDrills: TR-009 – First Exit After Defensive Regain
TR-014 – Stop the First Forward Disposal

title: Boundary or Corridor Choice
primarySkill: Selecting the appropriate exit lane after regaining possession.
objective: Teach players to choose between a fast corridor transition and a safer boundary exit according to pressure, numbers and available support.
groundSize: 55 metres long × 45 metres wide, divided into one corridor lane and two boundary lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the area into one central corridor lane and two boundary lanes.
Place a scoring gate at the end of each lane.
Divide players into two teams.
Begin play with the football entering a defensive contest near one end.
Position defenders and attackers differently for each repetition.
The coach controls the location and type of starting entry.
howTheDrillWorks:
The defending team attempts to regain possession from the starting entry.
Once possession is secured, players scan the three exit lanes.
The corridor gate is worth three points but may only be used when the receiver has clear separation.
Either boundary gate is worth one point and provides a lower-risk exit.
The opposition attempts to close one or more lanes.
The ball carrier and support players must recognise the open route.
A turnover in the corridor gives the opposition three points.
A retained boundary exit allows the team to continue attacking for an additional point.
The coach varies pressure so no lane is always preferred.
Reset after an exit, turnover or 30 seconds.
coachingPoints: Corridor use should be based on space, support and pressure.
Boundary exits can be effective when the corridor is closed.
Players must not treat wide movement as automatic failure.
The ball carrier should scan all three lanes.
Receivers must communicate whether they are genuinely free.
Far-side players should remain available for a switch.
The first disposal should not transfer pressure.
Team shape should support the selected lane.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players scan all exit lanes.
Whether corridor use is justified.
Whether boundary options are created early.
Whether the first receiver is under excessive pressure.
Whether the far side remains available.
Whether players adapt to changing defensive positioning.
Whether turnovers occur in high-risk central space.

commonErrors.error: Players force the corridor because it scores more points.
