commonErrors.correction: Deduct points for central turnovers and reinforce decision quality.

commonErrors.error: Players default to the boundary every time.
commonErrors.correction: Reward clear recognition of open central opportunities.

commonErrors.error: Outlet players wait until possession is secured before moving.
commonErrors.correction: Begin spreading as the regain is being completed.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier sees only the nearest side.
commonErrors.correction: Require scanning of corridor and opposite boundary.

commonErrors.error: Players choose a lane but fail to support it.
commonErrors.correction: Demand connected movement behind and ahead of the receiver.

progressions: Remove the lane cones.
Add full pressure.
Continue play to a scoring opportunity.
Add an opposition player behind each gate.
Introduce scoreboard and time conditions.
Require a switch after selected boundary exits.
regressions: Give the transitioning team an extra player.
Use only corridor and one boundary option.
successIndicators: Use the corridor when clearly open.
Select the boundary under central pressure.
Retain possession through the first transition phase.
matchApplication: A team exiting defence must balance the scoring potential of central ball movement against the danger of a corridor turnover. Effective players recognise when to attack directly and when to use the boundary to secure possession.
relatedDrills: TR-009 – First Exit After Defensive Regain

title: Transition Fundamentals Pressure Test
primarySkill: Applying transition fundamentals under continuous pressure.
objective: Assess whether players can consistently apply the first twenty transition concepts during continuous pressured play without relying on coach-directed solutions.
groundSize: 70 metres long × 50 metres wide with three scoring lanes at each end.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a large rectangular field.
Divide each end into a corridor scoring lane and two boundary scoring lanes.
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Position players across defensive, midfield and attacking lines.
Place spare footballs around the field.
Prepare an assessment sheet covering:
Recognition and communication
First-three-second action
Nearest-player pressure
Defensive fold
Corridor recovery
First-possession security
Outlet separation
Fast-or-secure decision
Boundary-or-corridor choice
Repeated support
howTheDrillWorks:
One team begins in possession and attacks towards its scoring end.
Play remains continuous through turnovers.
A corridor score is worth three points.
A boundary score is worth one point.
A team receives a transition bonus point when it demonstrates three correct transition actions in the same phase.
A defensive bonus point is awarded for preventing the first forward disposal.
An attacking bonus point is awarded for completing the first disposal and maintaining possession through the next two actions.
The coach introduces a new football when play becomes static.
Play four blocks of five minutes.
Provide only one coaching focus between blocks.
During the final block, remove all bonus scoring and assess natural behaviour.
Record team and individual transition outcomes after the session.
coachingPoints: Recognise and communicate the turnover immediately.
Apply nearest-player pressure without overcommitting numbers.
Fold defenders behind the pressure.
Protect the corridor and deepest dangerous space.
Secure the first possession before expanding.
Create forward, lateral and safety outlets.
Choose between fast attack and secure possession.
Select corridor or boundary exits according to pressure.
Continue supporting through multiple actions.
Maintain skill execution under fatigue.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Independent turnover recognition.
Quality and timing of communication.
Nearest-player pressure.
Defensive layering behind the pressure.
Corridor and deep-space protection.
Security of first possession and first disposal.
Separation of attacking outlets.
Quality of fast-or-secure decisions.
Selection of boundary or corridor exits.
Continued support after the first action.
Whether behaviours remain under fatigue.
Whether bonus behaviours transfer into unrestricted play.

commonErrors.error: Players rely on coach calls to recognise turnovers.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce coach communication and assess independent responses.

commonErrors.error: The defence pressures without folding behind.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce pressure, cover and deep roles.

commonErrors.error: The attacking team spreads before securing possession.
commonErrors.correction: Score the first clean possession and disposal separately.

commonErrors.error: Players force high-value corridor options.
commonErrors.correction: Penalise central turnovers and reward appropriate boundary use.

commonErrors.error: Support stops after the first disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Assess the complete transition chain through three actions.

commonErrors.error: Behaviours disappear during the unrestricted block.
commonErrors.correction: Review whether players understood the purpose or only chased bonus points.

progressions: Expand to full-ground play.
Allow match-like contact.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Create temporary numerical imbalance.
Start transitions from kick-ins, stoppages and forward-half turnovers.
Use video review and individual transition ratings.
Require positional groups to meet role-specific standards.
regressions: Reduce the field size and player numbers.
Give one team a numerical advantage.
Reduce running distances for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Reproduce the behaviours without bonus scoring.
matchApplication: This assessment tests whether transition fundamentals remain effective when players face realistic pressure, repeated turnovers, fatigue and changing field pictures. It provides a foundation before the chapter progresses into transition movement, pressure and advanced team systems.
relatedDrills: TR-014 – Stop the First Forward Disposal

title: Moving Turnover Trigger
primarySkill: Recognising and reacting to a turnover while already moving.
objective: Develop players’ ability to identify a possession change during continuous movement and immediately redirect their running into an appropriate attacking or defensive transition action.
groundSize: 40 metres long × 25 metres wide with two end gates and three movement channels.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Divide the area lengthways into three movement channels.
Place one scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams.
Position players throughout all three channels.
One team begins moving the football towards its attacking gate.
The opposition provides shadow pressure.
The coach stands centrally with spare footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team moves continuously through the channels using handball and short kicks.
All players must remain in motion and adjust their positioning as the football travels.
The coach creates a turnover by calling a team colour and feeding a new football to that team.
Every player must immediately change direction or transition role.
The team gaining possession spreads across the three channels and attacks the opposite gate.
The team losing possession applies nearest-player pressure and recovers towards the central channel.
A team receives one point if every player reacts within two seconds.
A second point is awarded if the new attacking team completes two disposals while remaining connected.
Progress to natural turnovers through interception.
Rotate starting positions every two minutes.
coachingPoints: Players should scan while moving rather than watching only the football.
The change of possession must produce an immediate change of direction.
The nearest defender pressures while others recover centrally.
The new attacking team should create width without becoming disconnected.
Players should accelerate out of the transition rather than jogging.
Movement should be purposeful and linked to team shape.
Communication must occur before players reach their new positions.
Players should maintain balance when changing direction at speed.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players recognise the turnover while moving.
The speed and balance of direction changes.
Whether attackers spread across useful lanes.
Whether defenders recover centrally.
Whether the nearest defender applies pressure.
Whether communication occurs during movement.
Whether players stop before changing direction.

commonErrors.error: Players stop before reacting.
commonErrors.correction: Require a continuous change of direction without becoming stationary.

commonErrors.error: Players turn only after seeing teammates move.
commonErrors.correction: Reward the first independent reactions after the turnover.

commonErrors.error: The new attacking team crowds one channel.
commonErrors.correction: Require occupation of all three channels.

commonErrors.error: Defenders continue chasing their previous opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Redirect off-ball defenders towards central recovery space.

commonErrors.error: Players lose balance when turning.
commonErrors.correction: Coach shorter steps and lower body position before acceleration.

progressions: Allow live interception.
Add touch pressure after the turnover.
Reduce the width of the channels.
Introduce a five-second scoring target.
Use two footballs to create unpredictable possession changes.
Remove the channel markers.
regressions: Stop play briefly before the new football is introduced.
successIndicators: Maintain connection through the first two disposals.
matchApplication: Turnovers often occur while players are already leading, chasing or supporting. Players must change direction and role immediately without waiting for a stoppage or becoming stationary.

title: Receive-and-Release on Regain
primarySkill: Receiving and releasing the football while moving after a regain.
objective: Develop players’ ability to receive at speed and complete a composed next disposal during defence-to-attack transition.
groundSize: 40 metres long × 25 metres wide with three receiving zones.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark three receiving zones in a staggered pattern.
Place one scoring gate at the far end.
Divide players into two teams.
Begin one team compact near the first zone.
Position the opposition around the outside under controlled pressure.
The coach begins each repetition with a loose football or intercept opportunity.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach feeds the football into the first contest area.
One team secures possession and immediately becomes the attacking team.
A teammate leads into the first receiving zone.
The receiver takes the football while moving and must release it before leaving the zone.
A second teammate leads into the next receiving zone.
The football continues through all three zones towards the scoring gate.
Defenders provide controlled tracking pressure.
One point is awarded for each clean moving receive-and-release.
Two bonus points are awarded for completing all three zones without slowing to a stop.
Roles reverse immediately if the football is intercepted.
coachingPoints: Receivers should move into space before calling for the football.
Hands and body should be prepared before the football arrives.
The receiver should scan the next option before taking possession.
Disposal should occur in rhythm rather than after stopping.
The ball carrier should place the football into the receiver’s running path.
Support runners should arrive at different angles.
Players should avoid leading directly towards the passer.
Skill execution must remain controlled despite speed.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether receivers lead into available space.
Whether they scan before receiving.
Whether the football is delivered into the running path.
Whether players remain balanced during disposal.
Whether the transition loses speed after each receive.
Whether defenders create realistic tracking pressure.
Whether support arrives in time for the next action.

commonErrors.error: Receivers stand and wait for the football.
commonErrors.correction: Require the lead to begin before the passer disposes.

commonErrors.error: Players receive and stop before releasing.
commonErrors.correction: Set a maximum of three moving steps inside each zone.

commonErrors.error: The receiver looks only at the incoming football.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage an early scan of the next option.

commonErrors.error: Passes are delivered behind the runner.
commonErrors.correction: Lead the receiver into space with the disposal.

commonErrors.error: Support players enter the same zone.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate separate receiving zones and angles.

progressions: Allow defenders to intercept.
Reduce the size of the receiving zones.
Require one kick and one handball in the chain.
Add a recovering defender from behind.
Remove the marked receiving zones.
Continue into a live scoring phase.
regressions: Allow receivers to slow before disposal.
matchApplication: Defence-to-attack transition relies on players receiving the football while moving into open space. Stopping after every possession allows the opposition to recover and close the next option.

title: Overlap After Turnover
primarySkill: Creating an overlap run after possession changes.
objective: Develop immediate overlap running that allows the team gaining possession to move past the first line of pressure.
groundSize: 45 metres long × 30 metres wide with two overlap channels.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a central possession area and one overlap channel on each side.
Place a scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams.
Begin one team in possession in the central area.
Position at least one player from each team near each side channel.
The coach holds spare footballs on the boundary.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team moves the football inside the central area.
When possession changes, the new ball winner releases to a nearby teammate.
The original ball winner immediately runs past the receiver into an overlap channel.
The receiver may return the football to the overlapping runner or use a different option.
The team scores one transition point for creating the overlap.
It receives a second point if the overlap breaks beyond the first defender.
Defenders attempt to pressure the receiver and track the runner.
If the opposition regains possession, it immediately creates its own overlap.
Continue play until a score or 30-second limit.
Rotate side-channel starting players every two minutes.
coachingPoints: The first disposer should accelerate immediately after releasing the football.
The overlap must pass the receiver at a useful angle.
The receiver should hold the defender before releasing.
The runner should communicate but avoid demanding the football when covered.
Other teammates must maintain width and depth.
The overlap should create advantage rather than unnecessary running.
Defenders should communicate whether to track or hand over.
Players must remain aware of counterattack risk if the overlap fails.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the first disposer runs immediately.
The angle and speed of the overlap.
Whether the receiver commits a defender.
Whether the overlapping runner is genuinely free.
Whether teammates maintain surrounding structure.
Whether defenders communicate tracking responsibility.
Whether players recover if the football turns over again.

commonErrors.error: The disposer stops after releasing.
commonErrors.correction: Make the overlap run compulsory for the first disposer.

commonErrors.error: The overlap runs directly behind the receiver.
commonErrors.correction: Use the outside shoulder and create a clear passing lane.

commonErrors.error: The receiver releases too early.
commonErrors.correction: Carry long enough to engage the first defender.

commonErrors.error: The runner calls while closely tracked.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage the receiver to use another option when the overlap is covered.

commonErrors.error: All teammates follow the overlap.
commonErrors.correction: Keep opposite-side width and a safety option behind.

progressions: Allow full tackling.
Remove the overlap channels.
Add a second overlapping runner.
Require the overlap to finish with a kick.
Introduce a recovering defender from behind.
Continue play into a full scoring zone.
regressions: Predetermine the side of the overlap.
Give the attacking team an extra player.
successIndicators: Recover quickly if possession is lost again.
matchApplication: An overlap run after a regain can exploit defenders who are still reacting to the turnover. It allows the team to move past immediate pressure before the opposition rebuilds its shape.

title: Defensive Chase-to-Cover
primarySkill: Changing from chasing the ball carrier to providing defensive cover.
objective: Teach defenders to recognise when direct pursuit is no longer effective and redirect their movement into a useful cover position.
groundSize: 45 metres long × 30 metres wide with three defensive cover zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark three defensive cover zones across the width of the field.
Place a scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams.
Begin one team in possession near the middle.
Position defenders at varied distances from the football.
The coach stands centrally with spare footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to move the football towards its scoring gate.
When a turnover occurs, the nearest former attacker pursues the ball carrier.
The next closest player assesses whether to continue chasing or move into a cover zone.
Once a teammate has established pressure, additional defenders must redirect into cover.
Defenders receive one point for occupying the correct cover zone before the next disposal.
They receive another point for intercepting or forcing a wide disposal.
Attackers receive two points for drawing several defenders to the football and using the space behind them.
Play continues for up to 30 seconds.
The coach varies the turnover location.
Rotate starting positions regularly.
coachingPoints: Not every defender should continue chasing the ball carrier.
Once pressure is established, supporting defenders must protect the next action.
Players should scan before changing their running line.
Cover should prioritise corridor and dangerous forward space.
Defenders must communicate role handovers.
Recovery angles should allow players to see ball and opponent.
Players should avoid running past useful defensive positions.
The team must preserve a deeper layer behind the contest.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether several defenders chase the same opponent.
Whether players scan before redirecting.
Whether cover zones are occupied early.
Whether the corridor remains protected.
Whether defenders communicate role handovers.
Whether a deeper defensive layer is preserved.
Whether attacking players exploit space behind overcommitted defenders.

commonErrors.error: Every defender continues chasing.
commonErrors.correction: Freeze play and identify which player already has pressure responsibility.

commonErrors.error: Players move into cover too early and concede easy possession.
commonErrors.correction: Ensure the nearest player establishes pressure before support folds away.

commonErrors.error: Cover players watch only the football.
commonErrors.correction: Scan the likely receiver and dangerous space.

commonErrors.error: Defenders recover directly behind the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Use angled runs into the next disposal lane.

commonErrors.error: Players fail to communicate handovers.
commonErrors.correction: Require clear “mine”, “cover” and “deep” calls.

progressions: Remove the marked cover zones.
Allow full tackling.
Give the attacking team a numerical advantage.
Add a second forward scoring gate.
Continue through repeated turnovers.
Add positional defensive responsibilities.
regressions: Give the defending team an extra player.
Keep fixed pressure and cover roles.
successIndicators: Identify when pressure is already established.
matchApplication: Defenders often waste energy chasing a player who is already under pressure. Redirecting into cover protects the next option and prevents the opposition from breaking through an overcommitted defensive line.
relatedDrills: TR-014 – Stop the First Forward Disposal

title: Moving Outlet Rotation
primarySkill: Rotating outlet positions while the football is moving.
objective: Develop continuous outlet movement so the ball carrier retains multiple transition options as the football changes location.
groundSize: 40 metres long × 35 metres wide with four rotating outlet zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark four outlet zones around a central playing area.
Divide players into two teams.
Place one or two players from each team near each outlet zone.
Begin with one team in possession in the centre.
The opposition provides controlled pressure.
The coach holds spare footballs outside the area.
howTheDrillWorks:
The team in possession attempts to move the football through an outlet zone.
Once the football enters one outlet zone, nearby support players rotate to create a new forward, lateral and safety shape.
The previously used outlet player must leave the zone and become support elsewhere.
No player may use the same outlet zone twice in succession.
When possession changes, the new attacking team immediately begins its own outlet rotation.
One point is awarded for exiting through a zone.
A bonus point is awarded for completing two different outlet rotations without losing possession.
Defenders attempt to anticipate and close the next outlet.
Continue play for 40-second periods.
Rotate players between central and outside roles.
coachingPoints: Outlet positions must move as the football moves.
Players should not remain fixed after their zone has been used.
The team must retain forward, lateral and safety support.
Rotations should create space rather than exchange positions without purpose.
Players should scan before moving into the next outlet.
Communication should identify occupied and open zones.
The ball carrier should avoid using a teammate moving into pressure.
Transition shape should remain connected throughout the rotation.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether outlet players remain stationary.
Whether rotations occur after each disposal.
Whether forward, lateral and safety options remain available.
Whether players move into open space.
Whether communication identifies the next outlet.
Whether the ball carrier scans before disposing.
Whether the team retains shape after a turnover.

commonErrors.error: Players remain in the same outlet zone.
commonErrors.correction: Require the used outlet player to rotate immediately.

commonErrors.error: Rotations cause players to cross and crowd.
commonErrors.correction: Use clear clockwise or space-based movement rules initially.

commonErrors.error: All support rotates ahead of the football.
commonErrors.correction: Keep one safety outlet behind the ball carrier.

commonErrors.error: Players rotate without scanning defenders.
commonErrors.correction: Make the next movement dependent on available space.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier waits for a preferred outlet.
commonErrors.correction: Use the best available option rather than delaying.

progressions: Remove the outlet-zone markers.
Increase defensive pressure.
Reduce the central area.
Require one opposite-side rotation.
Add a scoring gate after the second outlet.
Allow full tackling.
regressions: Keep players in fixed roles for several repetitions.
successIndicators: Rotate after an outlet is used.
matchApplication: As the football moves during transition, the best outlets continually change. Players must rotate and reposition rather than remaining where an earlier option existed.

title: Two-Way Transition Waves
primarySkill: Repeatedly transitioning in both directions.
objective: Develop the ability to repeatedly move from attack to defence and defence to attack during continuous end-to-end transition phases.
groundSize: 70 metres long × 40 metres wide with a scoring gate at each end.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a long rectangular field with a scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams.
Position players across defensive, midfield and attacking thirds.
Place spare footballs at both ends and along the centre.
The coach stands near the middle.
Begin with one team attacking from an end line.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team attacks towards the opposite scoring gate.
If the team scores, the coach immediately gives a new football to the defending team.
If the defending team regains possession, it counterattacks without stopping.
The former attacking team must recover defensively.
Play continues in repeated waves from end to end.
One point is awarded for reaching the scoring gate.
A bonus point is awarded for scoring within ten seconds of a regain.
The defending team receives a point for forcing a backwards disposal before the opposition crosses halfway.
Play in blocks of three to four minutes.
Rotate positional starting lines between blocks.
coachingPoints: Players must transition immediately after both scores and turnovers.
Support runners should maintain width and depth.
The nearest player pressures while teammates recover centrally.
Players should continue running after disposal.
Team shape must travel with the football.
Avoid all players sprinting ahead and leaving no protection behind.
Communication should continue despite fatigue.
Skill execution must remain composed at high speed.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players react after scoring.
Whether the former attacking team recovers immediately.
Whether support remains connected across the field.
Whether players maintain width.
Whether the nearest defender applies pressure.
Whether skill quality declines under fatigue.
Whether the same players repeatedly fail to run defensively.

commonErrors.error: Players celebrate or stop after scoring.
commonErrors.correction: Introduce the next football immediately and score defensive recovery.

commonErrors.error: Too many players run ahead of the football.
commonErrors.correction: Retain one or two players behind as safety support.

commonErrors.error: Defenders recover in straight lines without protecting the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Use angled recovery towards central space.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after giving a disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Require follow-up support into the next phase.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue causes rushed skill execution.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten blocks and demand composed decisions.

progressions: Add full tackling.
Reduce the field width.
Introduce numerical imbalance in selected waves.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Require a switch before scoring.
Continue for longer match-simulation blocks.
regressions: Reduce running requirements for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Transition after every score and turnover.
Repeat transition efforts across several waves.
matchApplication: Matches contain repeated transition phases rather than isolated turnovers. Players must attack, recover and attack again without waiting for structure to be reset by the coach.

title: Switch-and-Support Transition
primarySkill: Supporting a switch of play during transition.
objective: Develop coordinated far-side movement and support that allows the team gaining possession to switch away from pressure.
groundSize: 55 metres long × 45 metres wide with near-side and far-side transition lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the area into near-side, corridor and far-side lanes.
Place a scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams.
Begin each repetition with the football entering one side of the field.
Position the defending team compactly near the entry.
Position several potential outlet players on the opposite side.
The coach varies the starting side.
howTheDrillWorks:
The defending team attempts to regain possession near the starting side.
Once possession is secured, the team assesses whether the near-side exit is pressured.
If pressured, players circulate the football through a safety option towards the far side.
Far-side players hold width and then lead into receiving positions.
Support runners follow the switch to connect the next disposal.
Two points are awarded for completing the switch.
A bonus point is awarded for moving forward within two disposals after reaching the far side.
The opposition attempts to recover across the field and close the switch.
Roles reverse if the football turns over.
Reset after a score, boundary exit or 35 seconds.
coachingPoints: Far-side players must remain available before the switch begins.
The switch should move away from genuine pressure.
Safety support behind the football is essential.
Disposals should travel ahead of moving receivers.
The team must run to support after the switch.
Players should avoid switching slowly across exposed central space.
The ball carrier must scan the far side early.
Defenders should recover across without abandoning the corridor.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether far-side width is maintained.
Whether the ball carrier scans across the ground.
Whether safety support is available.
The speed and accuracy of the switch.
Whether players support the far-side receiver.
Whether the team moves forward after switching.
Whether defenders protect the corridor while recovering.

commonErrors.error: Far-side players drift towards the initial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width until the switch is clearly unavailable.

commonErrors.error: The switch is attempted without safety support.
commonErrors.correction: Require a player behind the football before changing sides.

commonErrors.error: The football moves slowly across the field.
commonErrors.correction: Use firm, direct disposals and moving receivers.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after completing the switch.
commonErrors.correction: Award the bonus only when the next forward action occurs.

commonErrors.error: The team forces a switch when the near side is open.
commonErrors.correction: Scan and use the best exit rather than a predetermined pattern.

progressions: Remove the lane markers.
Add full pressure.
Require a kick during the switch.
Add a recovering defender from the far side.
Continue into a full forward entry.
Introduce a time limit.
regressions: Use no defenders after the regain.
matchApplication: When pressure closes one side after a defensive regain, a fast switch can access open space before the opposition recovers. The switch is effective only when far-side players hold width and teammates support the next action.

title: Chain Through the Middle
primarySkill: Connecting moving disposals through the central part of the ground.
objective: Develop fast but controlled transition through the corridor using connected moving receivers and support runners.
groundSize: 60 metres long × 40 metres wide with a marked central corridor.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a corridor approximately 15 metres wide through the centre.
Place a scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams.
Begin with one team compact near a defensive regain zone.
Position defenders throughout the middle and attacking thirds.
The coach begins each repetition with a contested ball or intercept opportunity.
howTheDrillWorks:
The defending team secures possession in the regain zone.
Players scan for a moving receiver in the corridor.
The first corridor receiver must release to a second moving option.
A third support runner continues the chain towards the scoring gate.
The team receives one point for each completed corridor disposal.
Three bonus points are awarded for exiting the corridor into a scoring opportunity.
Defenders attempt to pressure from the side and close the next receiver.
If the corridor is closed, the attacking team may use a wide safety option.
Roles reverse immediately after a turnover.
Reset after a score, boundary exit or 30 seconds.
coachingPoints: Corridor movement must be based on clear space and support.
Receivers should arrive into the corridor rather than remain stationary within it.
Players must scan the next option before receiving.
Disposals should lead runners away from pressure.
Support must exist both ahead and behind the football.
The team should not force central play when the lane is closed.
Movement speed should exceed defensive recovery speed.
Players must protect against a central turnover.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether receivers move into central space at the correct time.
Whether they scan before possession.
Whether disposals lead the runner.
Whether support remains behind the football.
Whether players force covered corridor options.
Whether the chain maintains speed.
Whether the team reacts defensively after a central turnover.

commonErrors.error: Players stand in the corridor waiting.
commonErrors.correction: Require receivers to lead into the space as the previous disposal is made.

commonErrors.error: The first receiver turns into pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Scan before receiving and release in the direction of support.

commonErrors.error: Players force the corridor when closed.
commonErrors.correction: Use the wide safety outlet and rebuild.

commonErrors.error: The football is delivered behind moving receivers.
commonErrors.correction: Kick or handball into their running path.

commonErrors.error: No player remains behind the chain.
commonErrors.correction: Retain a safety runner to protect a turnover.

progressions: Reduce the corridor width.
Add full tackling.
Limit the number of corridor disposals.
Add a recovering defender from behind.
Remove the corridor markers.
Continue into a live inside-50 entry.
successIndicators: Exit wide when central pressure closes.
matchApplication: Fast corridor transition can create high-value attacking opportunities, but it requires precise movement, scanning and disposal. A central turnover is dangerous, so players must recognise when the chain is genuinely available.

title: Recover, Receive, Re-Enter
primarySkill: Recovering defensively and then rejoining the attacking transition.
objective: Develop players’ ability to complete a defensive recovery action and then immediately reposition as an attacking option after their team regains possession.
groundSize: 50 metres long × 35 metres wide with recovery and re-entry zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a recovery zone near each defensive end.
Mark a re-entry zone approximately 20 metres ahead of each recovery zone.
Place a scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams.
Begin one team attacking towards a gate.
Nominate two players from the attacking team as high support runners.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to score.
If possession is lost, the nominated high support runners must recover into their defensive recovery zone.
The nearest player pressures the new ball carrier.
If the team regains possession, the recovering players immediately change direction.
They must lead into the re-entry zone and become attacking options.
One point is awarded for completing the defensive recovery.
A second point is awarded if a recovering player receives during the next attacking transition.
The team receives two additional points for scoring after using a recovering player.
Roles reverse after each turnover.
Rotate nominated high support runners every two repetitions.
coachingPoints: High players must recover defensively when possession is lost.
Recovery should be purposeful rather than token running.
Players should scan for the moment possession is regained.
The change from recovery to attack must be immediate.
Re-entry runs should create a useful angle, not simply return to the previous position.
Teammates should recognise and use hard-working transition runners.
Players need enough energy control to perform both efforts.
Communication should indicate when to continue recovering or re-enter attack.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether high players recover after the turnover.
Whether they reach a useful defensive position.
Whether they recognise the regain.
The speed and angle of the re-entry run.
Whether teammates use the recovering player.
Whether fatigue affects skill quality.
Whether players stop after only one effort.

commonErrors.error: High players remain forward after possession is lost.
commonErrors.correction: Score only when they enter the defensive recovery zone.

commonErrors.error: Players recover but fail to turn when possession is regained.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate the regain and trigger immediate re-entry.

commonErrors.error: Re-entry runs return to congested space.
commonErrors.correction: Lead into a different lane or angle.

commonErrors.error: Teammates ignore the recovering runner.
commonErrors.correction: Award additional points for using the two-way runner.

commonErrors.error: Players sprint both ways without scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage regular shoulder checks during recovery.

progressions: Remove the marked zones.
Add full tackling.
Increase the recovery distance.
Require two players to re-enter the attack.
Continue through repeated turnovers.
Introduce positional running responsibilities.
regressions: Use one nominated runner per team.
Reduce running requirements for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Re-enter attack at a useful angle.
Contribute to the next possession chain.
matchApplication: Players who work back defensively are often well positioned to become free attacking options when possession is regained. Effective two-way runners contribute to both phases rather than stopping after one effort.

title: Transition Movement Assessment
primarySkill: Integrating movement-based transition behaviours under pressure.
objective: Assess whether players can execute coordinated movement, support and recovery actions during repeated live transitions.
groundSize: 75 metres long × 50 metres wide with a marked corridor and scoring zones.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a large rectangular field with a scoring zone at each end.
Mark a central corridor and two wide lanes.
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Position players across defensive, midfield and attacking lines.
Place spare footballs around the field.
Prepare an assessment sheet covering:
Reaction while moving
Moving receive-and-release
Overlap running
Chase-to-cover adjustment
Outlet rotation
Two-way transition running
Switch support
Corridor chain movement
Defensive recovery and attacking re-entry
howTheDrillWorks:
One team begins in possession and attacks towards its scoring zone.
Play remains live through all turnovers.
A team receives one point for entering the scoring zone and two points for scoring.
One movement bonus point is awarded for a successful overlap or moving receive-and-release.
One movement bonus point is awarded for completing a switch or corridor chain.
One defensive bonus point is awarded when a chasing player redirects into effective cover.
One two-way bonus point is awarded when a recovering player contributes to the next attacking phase.
The coach introduces a new football when play becomes static.
Play four blocks of five minutes.
Provide one movement-focused correction between blocks.
Remove all bonus scoring during the final block.
Compare natural behaviour with the scored blocks.
coachingPoints: Players must recognise turnovers while already moving.
Receivers should scan and release without stopping.
The first disposer should provide follow-up support.
Overlap runs must create a genuine advantage.
Outlets should rotate as the football changes location.
Defenders should change from pursuit to cover when pressure is established.
Players must work both ways through repeated transitions.
Switches and corridor chains require connected support.
Movement must remain purposeful under fatigue.
Skill quality should not be sacrificed for speed.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Reaction speed while players are moving.
Quality of moving receive-and-release actions.
Timing and effectiveness of overlaps.
Whether defenders redirect into cover.
Whether outlet players rotate.
Whether team shape travels with the football.
Whether far-side support enables switches.
Whether corridor chains remain controlled.
Whether recovering players re-enter attack.
Whether movement behaviours continue without bonus scoring.
Whether fatigue causes unnecessary stopping.
Whether skill execution remains composed.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after every possession.
commonErrors.correction: Reward continuous receive-and-release and follow-up running.

commonErrors.error: Overlap runs occur without creating advantage.
commonErrors.correction: Assess defender position before committing to the overlap.

commonErrors.error: Defenders all continue chasing.
commonErrors.correction: Redirect supporting defenders into cover roles.

commonErrors.error: Outlet positions remain fixed.
commonErrors.correction: Require rotation after each used option.

commonErrors.error: Players work hard in only one direction.
commonErrors.correction: Score defensive recovery and attacking re-entry.

commonErrors.error: Movement behaviours disappear in the final block.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce principles rather than dependence on bonus points.

progressions: Expand to full-ground match simulation.
Allow full match-like contact.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Introduce temporary numerical imbalance.
Require positional transition roles.
Add video review.
Extend continuous playing blocks.
regressions: Reduce field size and player numbers.
Reduce running distances for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Provide effective overlap and follow-up runs.
Reproduce movement behaviours during unrestricted play.
matchApplication: This assessment tests whether players can maintain effective movement during repeated possession changes. It prepares the group for more advanced transition work involving pressure, contests, tactical constraints and full-team systems.

title: Turnover Under Contact
primarySkill: Reacting to a turnover while under controlled physical pressure.
objective: Develop players’ ability to protect or regain the football and immediately perform the correct transition action when possession changes during physical contact.
groundSize: 30 metres long × 25 metres wide with two end scoring gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a rectangular playing area with a scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two balanced teams of four to eight.
Position players throughout the area rather than in fixed match-ups.
Begin with one team moving the football under controlled contact pressure.
The coach stands on the boundary with several spare footballs.
Establish clear legal-contact and tackling restrictions before beginning.
howTheDrillWorks:
The team in possession attempts to move the football through its attacking gate.
Defenders apply controlled body pressure and legal tackling.
When possession changes, the new ball carrier must first protect and stabilise the football.
The nearest former attacker applies immediate pressure.
Other former attackers recover towards the corridor and goal-side positions.
The new attacking team creates one close release, one forward option and one safety option.
The attacking team receives one point for securing the first possession and one point for completing the first disposal.
Two additional points are awarded for reaching the scoring gate.
The defending team receives two points for forcing an immediate secondary turnover.
Reset after a score, stoppage, boundary exit or 30 seconds.
coachingPoints: Players must maintain strong body position through contact.
The ball winner should secure possession before attempting an ambitious disposal.
The nearest defender pressures without conceding an avoidable free kick.
Supporting defenders protect likely exits rather than all joining the tackle.
Attacking support should arrive from different angles.
Players must communicate through the contact phase.
The transition response begins before the contest is fully resolved.
Players should recover their balance quickly after contact.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Body position during contact.
Whether the ball winner protects the football.
Whether the first disposal is composed.
Whether the nearest defender reacts immediately.
Whether supporting defenders recover instead of overcommitting.
Whether attacking support is available.
Whether contact remains legal and controlled.
Whether players remain involved after the initial contest.

commonErrors.error: The ball winner disposes blindly while being contacted.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the football, stabilise the body and identify a clear receiver.

commonErrors.error: Multiple defenders join the same tackle.
commonErrors.correction: Assign the nearest player to contact and others to cover outlets.

commonErrors.error: Players appeal for a decision after losing possession.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce immediate transition regardless of the expected umpire call.

commonErrors.error: Support players stand too close to the contact.
commonErrors.correction: Create one close release and maintain wider exit options.

commonErrors.error: Contact intensity becomes unsafe.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce pressure, reset technique and reinforce legal tackling standards.

progressions: Increase pressure to controlled match-like tackling.
Reduce the size of the playing area.
Add a three-second scoring window after the regain.
Create temporary numerical disadvantage for the team winning possession.
Require the first disposal to travel forward when a clear option exists.
Continue play through repeated turnovers.
regressions: Use touch or wrap-up tackling only.
Increase the size of the area.
Give the ball-winning team an extra support player.
Stop briefly after the initial contest.
Begin with one-on-one or two-on-two contests.
Reduce contact and running demands for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Apply immediate legal pressure after losing possession.
matchApplication: Many AFL turnovers occur during tackles, contested ground balls and physical pressure. Players must remain composed through contact and immediately transition when the football changes hands.

title: Loose-Ball Transition Scramble
primarySkill: Transitioning from an unpredictable loose-ball contest.
objective: Develop rapid attack-to-defence and defence-to-attack reactions when possession changes repeatedly around an unpredictable loose football.
groundSize: 25 metres long × 25 metres wide with four outside release gates.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a central contest square measuring approximately 18 metres × 18 metres.
Place one release gate outside each side of the square.
Divide players into two teams of four to seven.
Position players around and inside the central square.
The coach stands outside the area with several footballs.
Begin with controlled contact and clear ground-ball safety rules.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach rolls, bounces or deflects the football unpredictably into the square.
Both teams contest for possession.
Possession may change several times before one team secures the football.
Every change of possession requires immediate pressure from the nearest opponent.
The team with stable possession attempts to exit through any release gate.
One point is awarded for the initial clean possession.
One additional point is awarded for a successful first disposal.
Two points are awarded for exiting through a gate.
If the football is turned over again, scoring responsibility immediately changes.
Reset after an exit, stoppage, boundary departure or 25 seconds.
coachingPoints: Players should stay low and balanced around the loose football.
The nearest teammate supports the ball winner without crowding.
Players must distinguish between a brief touch and genuine possession.
Pressure begins immediately when an opponent controls the football.
Outside players should hold useful release positions.
Blind kicks and handballs should be avoided.
Communication should identify possession, pressure and available gates.
Players must continue reacting through repeated changes of possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Ground-ball body position.
Whether players recognise stable possession.
Whether support is available without overcrowding.
Whether pressure changes with each turnover.
Whether outside outlets remain separated.
Whether players use composed first disposals.
Whether effort continues through multiple possession changes.

commonErrors.error: Players stand upright around the loose football.
commonErrors.correction: Lower the body and approach with hands prepared.

commonErrors.error: Teammates crowd the ball winner.
commonErrors.correction: Keep one close support player and others outside the contest.

commonErrors.error: Players stop when the opposition briefly touches the football.
commonErrors.correction: React to confirmed possession while remaining ready for another change.

commonErrors.error: Blind disposals create immediate turnovers.
commonErrors.correction: Protect possession and locate a clear release target.

commonErrors.error: Players remain focused on the original attacking direction.
commonErrors.correction: Reidentify the scoring gate after every change of possession.

progressions: Reduce the size of the square.
Increase contact to controlled match-like pressure.
Close one release gate after possession is won.
Require two completed disposals before exiting.
Add a five-second limit after stable possession.
Continue into a larger transition area after the exit.
regressions: Give one team a numerical advantage.
Place stationary support players outside the gates.
Shorten work periods for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Compete safely and effectively for the loose football.
matchApplication: Loose footballs often create several rapid possession changes before one team gains control. Players must repeatedly reassess attacking and defensive roles rather than assuming the contest is finished after the first touch.

title: Outnumbered Recovery Race
primarySkill: Recovering defensively when temporarily outnumbered.
objective: Develop defensive transition decisions that slow an opposition counterattack and protect dangerous space until recovering teammates restore numerical balance.
groundSize: 45 metres long × 30 metres wide with a scoring gate at each end.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a rectangular field with a scoring gate at each end.
Begin three attackers against two defenders inside the playing area.
Position two recovering defenders five to ten metres behind the attacking group.
Place a coach with footballs near the starting end.
Rotate players through attacking, initial-defending and recovery roles.
Adjust recovery distances according to age and conditioning level.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach gives possession to the attacking group.
Three attackers advance towards the scoring gate against two initial defenders.
Recovering defenders begin chasing as soon as the first disposal is made.
The nearest initial defender pressures or delays the ball carrier.
The second initial defender protects the most dangerous central option.
Recovering defenders sprint goal-side and communicate their arrival.
Attackers score two points by reaching the gate before defensive balance is restored.
Defenders score one point for forcing a sideways or backwards disposal.
Defenders score two points for restoring equal numbers and three for regaining possession.
Reset after a score, turnover or 20-second limit.
coachingPoints: Outnumbered defenders should delay rather than overcommit.
Protect the corridor and deepest dangerous attacker.
Force the attack to use additional disposals.
Recovering players must sprint to goal-side positions.
Communication should identify who pressures and who covers.
Defenders should avoid both committing to the ball carrier.
Once numbers are restored, the defence can become more aggressive.
Attackers should recognise and exploit the temporary advantage quickly.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the nearest defender controls the ball carrier.
Whether the second defender protects the central option.
The speed and angle of recovery runs.
Whether defenders communicate role changes.
Whether the attack is forced to use extra disposals.
Whether recovering players stop after reaching the contest.
Whether defenders become aggressive once numbers are restored.

commonErrors.error: The first defender charges and is bypassed.
commonErrors.correction: Close space under control and delay the ball carrier.

commonErrors.error: Both defenders engage the same attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Keep one defender protecting the central receiver.

commonErrors.error: Recovering players chase directly from behind.
commonErrors.correction: Angle recovery towards goal-side and corridor positions.

commonErrors.error: Defenders attempt an intercept that opens the scoring gate.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise delay and central protection.

commonErrors.error: Attackers hold the football and allow recovery.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage early forward movement while numbers favour the attack.

progressions: Increase the initial attacking advantage.
Add controlled tackling.
Widen the playing area.
Delay the recovering defenders by an additional second.
Continue play in the opposite direction after a defensive regain.
Add a second scoring option for the attackers.
regressions: Allow one recovering defender to start earlier.
Reduce distances and repeat efforts for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Regain possession without conceding a direct score.
matchApplication: Turnovers often leave defenders temporarily outnumbered. Effective delay and recovery can prevent a fast score and give teammates enough time to rebuild defensive structure.

title: Crowded Regain Exit
primarySkill: Exiting congestion after regaining possession.
objective: Develop a composed first-possession and support pattern that allows a team to escape congestion and begin transition without immediately returning the football to the opposition.
groundSize: A 15-metre central congestion square inside a 35-metre × 30-metre transition area.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central congestion square measuring approximately 15 metres × 15 metres.
Place four exit gates around the outside transition area.
Position three to five players from each team inside the square.
Position one outside support player from each team beyond the square.
The coach stands beside the square with spare footballs.
Establish controlled tackling and safe congestion rules.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach feeds the football into the congestion square.
Players contest until one team secures possession.
The ball winner may use one close handball inside the square.
The next disposal should release the football to an outside support player when possible.
Outside players reposition to create separated exit options.
The team receives one point for securing possession.
A second point is awarded for releasing the football outside the square.
Two additional points are awarded for exiting through a gate.
The opposition attempts to force a turnover before the exit.
Reset after a successful exit, stoppage or 25 seconds.
coachingPoints: The ball winner should protect possession and keep the arms free.
Close support should be visible and moving.
Players must avoid handballing to a stationary teammate under equal pressure.
Outside support should hold width and communicate.
The first release should reduce congestion.
Players should not force a kick directly from heavy pressure.
Support runners must continue after the football leaves the square.
The team should spread once control is established.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Body position in congestion.
Whether the ball winner protects the football.
Whether close support is genuinely available.
Whether disposals reduce or transfer pressure.
Whether outside players maintain separation.
Whether the football exits the congested area cleanly.
Whether the team continues supporting after release.

commonErrors.error: The ball winner throws the football onto the boot blindly.
commonErrors.correction: Protect possession and locate a handball release.

commonErrors.error: Players handball to a teammate under greater pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Choose a receiver who can move the football away from congestion.

commonErrors.error: Outside support enters the square.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width and provide a visible exit target.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after the ball leaves congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Continue supporting towards the exit gate.

commonErrors.error: The release player receives flat-footed.
commonErrors.correction: Lead into space and receive while moving.

progressions: Reduce the congestion square.
Increase contact pressure.
Remove the nominated outside support players.
Close one exit gate after possession is won.
Require a kick after the football leaves the square.
Continue into a larger live transition phase.
regressions: Reduce player numbers inside the square.
Give the ball-winning team an extra outside player.
Allow the coach to nominate the exit side.
Remove contact for younger or returning players.
successIndicators: Move the football out of congestion.
Maintain support beyond the first release.
matchApplication: Defensive regains often occur in crowded areas near stoppages, spoils or forward pressure. A clean release from congestion allows the team to access space before the opposition can lock the football back inside.

title: Repeat Pressure Lock-In
primarySkill: Maintaining repeat defensive pressure after losing possession.
objective: Develop multiple consecutive defensive efforts that prevent the opposition from escaping after a turnover.
groundSize: 40 metres long × 35 metres wide with a central lock-in zone and four exit gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central playing area with one exit gate on each side.
Divide players into two teams of five to nine.
One team begins in possession and attempts to exit.
The defending team begins in a compact shape around the football.
The coach holds spare footballs around the boundary.
Use short, high-intensity repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The team in possession attempts to complete an exit through any gate.
The defending team applies immediate pressure and closes likely outlets.
If the attackers complete a disposal but remain inside the area, a new defender must become the primary pressure player.
Other defenders fold behind and protect the next options.
The defence receives one point for each forced sideways or backwards disposal.
Two points are awarded for forcing a stoppage.
Three points are awarded for regaining possession.
The attacking team receives three points for a controlled exit.
Repetitions last a maximum of 25 seconds.
Swap attacking and defending roles after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Pressure must continue beyond the first effort.
The nearest defender changes as the football moves.
Players who have pressured must recover into cover.
Defenders should close central and forward exits first.
Communication must identify the next pressure player.
The group should avoid several defenders chasing the same receiver.
Pressure should remain controlled enough to prevent evasion.
Work rate must support tactical shape rather than become random chasing.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether pressure continues after the first disposal.
Whether the nearest defender changes correctly.
Whether previous pressure players fold into cover.
Whether forward and central exits are closed.
Whether defenders maintain legal contact.
Whether communication remains clear under fatigue.
Whether effort becomes disorganised chasing.

commonErrors.error: Defenders stop after the first pressure effort.
commonErrors.correction: Score each consecutive pressure action and require immediate recovery.

commonErrors.error: The same defender chases every disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Transfer pressure responsibility to the nearest teammate.

commonErrors.error: Multiple defenders collapse on one receiver.
commonErrors.correction: Keep supporting defenders on likely exits.

commonErrors.error: Pressure players run past the receiver.
commonErrors.correction: Close quickly and shorten steps before contact.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue causes the defensive shape to disappear.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten repetitions and reinforce pressure, cover and balance.

progressions: Reduce the playing area.
Increase contact to match-like legal pressure.
Add a fifth exit that opens unpredictably.
Require the attacking team to use both kick and handball.
Continue into a counterattack after the defence regains possession.
Increase repetition length for advanced groups.
regressions: Give the defence an extra player.
Pause briefly after each disposal to reset roles.
Reduce repetition length for Over 35 players.
matchApplication: One pressure effort rarely wins the football. Teams must repeatedly pressure receivers, fold behind the ball and close exits to prevent the opposition escaping after a turnover.
relatedDrills: TR-014 – Stop the First Forward Disposal

title: Contested Switch Escape
primarySkill: Switching away from concentrated opposition pressure after a contested regain.
objective: Develop the ability to secure a pressured regain and transfer the football to the far side before the opposition can lock the contest in.
groundSize: 50 metres long × 45 metres wide with a contested near-side zone and far-side exit gate.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a contested starting zone near one boundary.
Place a narrow near-side exit and a wider far-side exit.
Position three to five players from each team near the starting zone.
Position additional players across the corridor and far side.
The coach begins each repetition with a high ball, ground ball or pressured pass.
Alternate the starting side regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
Both teams contest for the starting football.
Once a team gains possession, the opposition applies immediate pressure.
The ball-winning team may use a close release to escape the contest.
Players behind and across the football create a switch pathway.
Far-side players maintain width and lead into space.
One point is awarded for securing the regain.
Two points are awarded for transferring the football beyond the corridor.
Three points are awarded for exiting through the far-side gate.
The opposition receives three points for forcing a turnover before the switch.
Reset after an exit, turnover, stoppage or 30 seconds.
coachingPoints: Possession must be secured before the switch begins.
A safety player behind the football starts the change of direction.
Far-side players should hold width until the football is ready to travel.
The switch should move quickly enough to beat defensive recovery.
Players must avoid slow, exposed disposals across central space.
The near-side exit remains available if the switch is not safe.
Support runners should follow the football across the field.
The ball carrier must scan the far side early.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the regain is controlled.
Whether safety support is available.
Whether far-side width is preserved.
The speed and accuracy of the switch.
Whether the opposition closes the central pathway.
Whether players recognise when the near-side exit is safer.
Whether support follows the football after the switch.

commonErrors.error: The switch begins before possession is stable.
commonErrors.correction: Complete a secure release before changing sides.

commonErrors.error: Far-side players move into the initial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width and remain available outside pressure.

commonErrors.error: Disposals across the ground are slow or floating.
commonErrors.correction: Use firm, direct delivery to moving receivers.

commonErrors.error: Players force the far-side exit when covered.
commonErrors.correction: Retain the near-side safety option.

commonErrors.error: Support remains on the original side.
commonErrors.correction: Run across behind and ahead of the football.

progressions: Remove the marked switch pathway.
Add full controlled tackling.
Reduce the time allowed to reach the far side.
Add a recovering defender from the far-side gate.
Continue into a forward-entry phase.
Vary the location and type of contested regain.
regressions: Remove pressure after the first release.
Give the transitioning team an extra player.
Reduce physical pressure for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Create a safe release behind the football.
Transfer the football quickly and accurately.
Support the switch across the field.
Use the safer exit when the switch is closed.
matchApplication: When a defensive regain occurs near the boundary under heavy pressure, the opposite side may contain the best attacking space. A secure and supported switch can escape the opposition’s pressure zone.

title: Tackle-to-Counterattack
primarySkill: Converting a successful tackle or pressure action into an immediate counterattack.
objective: Develop the ability to move immediately from a successful defensive pressure action into a secure and organised attacking transition.
groundSize: 35 metres long × 30 metres wide with two end gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a rectangular field with one scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams of four to eight.
Begin with one team carrying and disposing under controlled pressure.
Position teammates around the ball carrier to create realistic support.
The coach stands outside the area with spare footballs.
Rehearse safe tackle technique before live repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to move the football towards its scoring gate.
Defenders apply legal controlled tackling and pressure.
If a tackle causes a free kick, spill or turnover, the defending team immediately becomes the attacking team.
The tackler either receives the free kick or recovers into support.
Teammates spread into forward, lateral and safety options.
One point is awarded for creating the turnover.
One point is awarded for completing the first disposal.
Two points are awarded for reaching the opposite scoring gate.
The former attacking team must immediately apply transition pressure.
Reset after a score, stoppage or 30 seconds.
coachingPoints: Tackles must be legal, controlled and technically sound.
Players should anticipate where a pressured football may spill.
The tackler must recover quickly after completing the action.
Teammates should spread as soon as possession is won.
The first disposal must reduce pressure.
Former attackers must react rather than appealing to the umpire.
Players should communicate ownership of the loose football.
The team must continue beyond the turnover-winning action.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Tackle safety and legality.
Whether supporting defenders anticipate the spill.
Whether the tackler recovers quickly.
Whether attacking shape forms after the regain.
Whether the first disposal is secure.
Whether the former attacking team reacts defensively.
Whether players celebrate the tackle instead of continuing play.

commonErrors.error: The tackler remains on the ground after completing the tackle.
commonErrors.correction: Release safely, regain the feet and become support.

commonErrors.error: Teammates watch the tackle instead of preparing for the spill.
commonErrors.correction: Position one player front-and-centre and others around likely exits.

commonErrors.error: The new attacking team crowds the football.
commonErrors.correction: Create separated forward, lateral and safety outlets.

commonErrors.error: The ball winner kicks blindly after the spill.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession and identify a clear receiver.

commonErrors.error: Former attackers appeal rather than defend.
commonErrors.correction: Continue play regardless of the expected decision.

progressions: Increase contact to match-like controlled tackling.
Reduce the playing area.
Add a five-second scoring bonus after the turnover.
Allow the attacking team a numerical advantage.
Continue through repeated turnover phases.
Add positional starting roles.
regressions: Begin with tackle-bag or wrap-up technique.
Give the new attacking team a neutral support player.
Reduce contact and repeat efforts for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Recover the spilled football or free kick.
matchApplication: A successful tackle creates value only when the team secures the resulting possession and moves the football before the opposition can recover. Players must transition immediately from pressure to attack.

title: Aerial Contest Transition
primarySkill: Transitioning from the outcome of an aerial contest.
objective: Develop coordinated attacking and defensive transition responses following a mark, spoil or ground-ball outcome from an aerial contest.
groundSize: 45 metres long × 35 metres wide with an aerial-contest zone and scoring gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central aerial-contest zone approximately 15 metres × 15 metres.
Place one scoring gate at each end of the wider area.
Position one aerial contestant from each team inside the zone.
Position teammates around the contest in front-and-centre, defensive and outlet positions.
The coach begins each repetition with a high kick.
Rotate aerial contestants regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach kicks the football into the aerial-contest zone.
Players compete to mark or spoil.
If a mark is taken, the marking team immediately spreads and attacks its gate.
If the football is spoiled, ground-level players compete for possession.
The team winning the loose football transitions into attack.
The team losing the contest applies nearest-player pressure and recovers centrally.
One point is awarded for winning the aerial or ground-level outcome.
One point is awarded for completing the first disposal.
Two points are awarded for reaching the scoring gate.
Reset after a score, turnover or 30 seconds.
coachingPoints: Ground-level players should anticipate likely spoil directions.
Players must react to the actual outcome rather than assuming a mark or spoil.
A marking player should scan quickly before moving the football.
The team winning possession should spread from the contest.
The losing team should pressure the ball and protect the corridor.
Front-and-centre positioning is essential beneath the contest.
Players behind the contest should provide defensive balance or safety support.
Aerial contact must remain legal and appropriately controlled.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Positioning around the aerial contest.
Whether players anticipate the spoil.
Whether players react immediately to a mark or loose ball.
Whether the first disposal is composed.
Whether attacking width is created.
Whether defenders pressure and recover centrally.
Whether aerial and ground-level contact remains safe.

commonErrors.error: Ground players stand directly under the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Position front-and-centre and behind the expected spoil.

commonErrors.error: Players assume their teammate will mark.
commonErrors.correction: Prepare for all possible outcomes until possession is secured.

commonErrors.error: The marking player disposes without scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Take a quick field scan before selecting the outlet.

commonErrors.error: Players crowd the contest after possession is won.
commonErrors.correction: Spread to forward, wide and safety positions.

commonErrors.error: Defenders watch the aerial contest and react late.
commonErrors.correction: Begin transition movement as the outcome becomes clear.

progressions: Vary kick height, direction and distance.
Allow stronger controlled aerial bodywork.
Add an extra ground-level player to each team.
Require a switch after selected regains.
Continue into a full forward-entry phase.
Introduce repeated aerial contests without resetting.
regressions: Use uncontested marking followed by live transition.
Increase the size of the contest zone.
Shorten running distances for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Position correctly around the aerial contest.
Pressure and recover after losing the contest.
matchApplication: Aerial contests regularly produce immediate changes of possession. Players around the contest must read the outcome and transition before the opposition can exploit the loose or newly controlled football.
relatedDrills: SP-001 – Balanced Aerial Defence Starting Position

title: Pressure Exit Decision
primarySkill: Selecting the safest effective exit while under heavy pressure.
objective: Develop composed exit decisions after a regain when pressure, space and available teammates change rapidly.
groundSize: 45 metres long × 40 metres wide with four differently valued exit gates.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a central regain zone.
Place a corridor gate, two boundary gates and one rear safety gate around the area.
Assign three points to the corridor gate, two to the opposite boundary, one to the near boundary and no scoring value to the rear safety gate.
Divide players into two teams.
Position defenders so different gates are pressured each repetition.
The coach starts play with varied contested or intercepted footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players contest or receive the starting football inside the regain zone.
The team gaining possession scans all four exits.
The opposition applies immediate pressure and attempts to close the highest-value options.
The ball-winning team may use the rear safety gate to retain possession without scoring.
A successful controlled exit scores the listed gate value.
A turnover through the corridor gives the opposition three points.
A turnover through a boundary option gives the opposition one point.
The coach changes defensive starting positions each repetition.
Players briefly identify why they selected an exit during recovery.
Reset after an exit, turnover or 25 seconds.
coachingPoints: Gate value should not replace decision quality.
The ball carrier must assess pressure, support and turnover consequence.
A safe reset can be the correct decision.
The corridor should be used only with clear separation and support.
Boundary options reduce central turnover risk.
Teammates must communicate honestly when covered.
The first disposal should improve the next player’s situation.
Players should scan before taking full possession whenever possible.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players scan all gates.
Whether high-value options are forced.
Whether the rear safety option is used appropriately.
Whether receivers communicate pressure.
Whether the first disposal improves field position or possession security.
Whether players understand turnover consequence.
Whether decisions change as defensive positioning changes.

commonErrors.error: Players always choose the three-point corridor gate.
commonErrors.correction: Penalise central turnovers and review the actual pressure picture.

commonErrors.error: Players always use the rear safety gate.
commonErrors.correction: Reward recognition of genuine forward or wide opportunities.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier selects an exit before gaining possession.
commonErrors.correction: Scan early but confirm the option after securing the football.

commonErrors.error: Receivers call despite being covered.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate only when a safe receiving lane exists.

commonErrors.error: The first disposal transfers pressure to a stationary teammate.
commonErrors.correction: Select a moving receiver with time and space.

progressions: Remove gate values and assess decisions subjectively.
Remove the gate markers.
Add match-like contact.
Introduce scoreboard and time scenarios.
Continue play beyond the first exit.
Give the defending team delayed recovering players.
regressions: Allow the coach to pause play before the decision.
Give the transitioning team an extra player.
successIndicators: Match decisions to pressure and support.
Explain the reasoning behind selected exits.
matchApplication: A defensive regain may present several possible exits with different rewards and risks. Effective players choose the option most likely to retain possession and begin attack, rather than automatically selecting the shortest or most aggressive route.

title: Transition Contest Assessment
primarySkill: Integrating transition behaviours following pressured and contested possession changes.
objective: Assess whether players can apply transition fundamentals and movement principles when turnovers occur through contact, congestion, loose footballs and aerial contests.
groundSize: 75 metres long × 55 metres wide with central, boundary and aerial-contest zones.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a large field with one scoring zone at each end.
Mark a central congestion zone, two boundary exit lanes and one aerial-contest zone.
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Position players across defensive, midfield and attacking lines.
Place spare footballs at several field locations.
Prepare an assessment sheet covering:
Turnover recognition under pressure
First-possession security
Nearest-player pressure
Outnumbered recovery
Congestion exit
Repeat pressure
Contested switch
Tackle-to-counterattack
Aerial-contest transition
Pressure exit decision
howTheDrillWorks:
One team begins in possession and attacks towards its scoring zone.
Play remains continuous through all natural turnovers.
The coach periodically introduces a new football through a loose-ball, aerial or congested starting situation.
One point is awarded for entering the scoring zone and two for scoring.
A transition bonus point is awarded for securing the first possession and completing the first disposal.
A defensive bonus point is awarded for repeat pressure that forces a backwards disposal, stoppage or turnover.
An outnumbered-recovery bonus is awarded when defenders delay until numerical balance is restored.
An exit-decision bonus is awarded when a team selects the most appropriate available route.
Play four blocks of five minutes with brief feedback between blocks.
Vary the turnover type in each block.
