primarySkill: Manipulating changing numerical advantages during continuous transition.
objective: Develop team recognition and use of changing numerical balance as players enter, leave or recover during continuous transition phases.
groundSize: 80 metres long × 50 metres wide with entry gates along both boundaries.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a long rectangular field with a scoring gate at each end.
Place two player-entry gates on each boundary.
Divide players into two teams with substitutes waiting at the gates.
Begin with equal numbers on the field.
The coach uses number cards or verbal calls to send additional players into selected phases.
Players are not told in advance which team will gain the numerical advantage.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team begins in possession and attacks towards its gate.
During play, the coach releases one or more players through an entry gate.
The arriving player may create attacking advantage, defensive balance or temporary overload.
Players must communicate the new numbers.
The team with advantage attempts to use the spare quickly.
The team at disadvantage delays and protects central space.
One point is awarded for identifying the spare player.
Two points are awarded for using an advantage to break a line.
The disadvantaged team receives two points for delaying until numbers equalise.
The coach may then release another player to change the balance again.
Play continues for up to 60 seconds.
Reset and rotate entry players after each wave.
coachingPoints: Numerical balance must be reassessed continuously.
Arriving players should enter into useful space.
The spare player should not move towards congestion.
The ball carrier should commit a defender before releasing.
Outnumbered defenders must delay rather than gamble.
Central and deepest threats remain defensive priorities.
Communication should include actual numbers where practical.
Players must adjust immediately when the balance changes again.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players recognise numerical changes.
Whether arriving players create useful shape.
Whether the spare player is identified.
Whether defenders delay appropriately.
Whether players continue using an old numerical picture.
Whether communication is specific.
Whether role rotation occurs when numbers equalise.

commonErrors.error: Players fail to notice an entering player.
commonErrors.correction: Scan outside the immediate contest and communicate the count.

commonErrors.error: The new player runs directly to the football.
commonErrors.correction: Enter into the space that creates or restores balance.

commonErrors.error: The attacking team uses excessive disposals before finding the spare.
commonErrors.correction: Commit one defender and release quickly.

commonErrors.error: Outnumbered defenders attempt risky intercepts.
commonErrors.correction: Delay, protect the corridor and wait for support.

commonErrors.error: Players do not adjust when another player enters.
commonErrors.correction: Recount and reorganise after every numerical change.

progressions: Release players without verbal warning.
Add full match-like pressure.
Change numbers more than once during a phase.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Expand to full-ground transition.
Require position-specific entry roles.
regressions: Shorten the playing waves for Over 35 players.
matchApplication: Player numbers around the football change constantly as teammates recover, overlap or leave contests. Elite transition depends on recognising and exploiting temporary numerical advantages before they disappear.

title: Floating Player Transition Rotation
primarySkill: Integrating a floating player without losing team balance.
objective: Develop coordinated use of a floating transition player while ensuring teammates rotate to maintain width, line connection and defensive security.
groundSize: 75 metres long × 50 metres wide with defensive, midfield and attacking thirds.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the field into defensive, midfield and attacking thirds.
Divide players into two teams.
Add one neutral floating player who supports the team in possession.
The floating player may move anywhere.
Begin each phase with a defensive or midfield regain.
Require teams to maintain at least two players behind the football.
Rotate the floating role every three minutes.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team gains possession and may use the floating player.
The floating player moves to become the most useful transition connection.
A teammate must rotate to preserve team width or security when the float moves.
The team receives one point for using the float to complete a line-breaking possession.
One point is awarded for a successful role rotation around the float.
Two points are awarded for entering the attacking third.
Two additional points are awarded for scoring.
If the football turns over, the float immediately supports the new attacking team.
Both teams must reorganise around the float’s new position.
A turnover caused by losing behind-ball security gives the opposition a bonus point.
Play in three-minute blocks.
Rotate the float and restart from varied locations.
coachingPoints: The floating player should move to solve the current transition problem.
Teammates must not simply follow the float.
When the float moves forward, another player may need to replace behind.
When the float moves wide, central connection must remain.
The float should communicate the role being provided.
Players must reorganise immediately after a turnover.
The team should avoid overusing the neutral player when direct options exist.
The float must receive in space with a clear next action.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the float moves to a useful location.
Whether teammates rotate around the movement.
Whether width and security are preserved.
Whether the team overuses the floating player.
Whether the float has a next option.
Whether teams reorganise after turnovers.
Whether the float communicates the role being provided.

commonErrors.error: Teammates crowd around the floating player.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain normal spacing and use the float as one option.

commonErrors.error: The float runs ahead and leaves no security.
commonErrors.correction: Require a teammate to replace behind before the movement continues.

commonErrors.error: Players automatically dispose to the neutral player.
commonErrors.correction: Use direct team options when they provide greater advantage.

commonErrors.error: The float receives without a next action.
commonErrors.correction: Move into positions that connect at least two teammates or lines.

commonErrors.error: Teams react slowly when the float changes sides after turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Reorganise immediately around the new possession team.

progressions: Add a second floating player with different movement restrictions.
Limit the number of float possessions.
Add full match-like pressure.
Remove the marked thirds.
Introduce scoreboard and time conditions.
Allow the defending team to temporarily deny the float.
regressions: Restrict the float to the midfield third.
Stop after turnovers to review rotations.
Keep three players behind the football.
Use shorter blocks for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Use the float to connect lines or break pressure.
matchApplication: Some players naturally become transition connectors by moving across positional lines. The team must use their movement without abandoning width, role balance or protection behind the football.

title: High-Risk Transition Protection
primarySkill: Protecting the team while attempting an aggressive transition option.
objective: Develop coordinated protection behind the football when the team attempts a high-reward corridor kick, overlap, switch or line-breaking disposal.
groundSize: 90 metres long × 60 metres wide using full-width transition space.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use a large field with one scoring zone at each end.
Mark high-risk target areas through the corridor and opposite side.
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Require the attacking team to maintain at least two security players behind the football.
Position defenders to create genuine interception opportunities.
Begin each phase with a defensive or midfield regain.
The coach may nominate when an aggressive option becomes available.
howTheDrillWorks:
The team gaining possession begins a normal transition.
A high-risk option may appear through the corridor, switch or overlap.
Before the disposal is made, players behind the football organise turnover protection.
The team receives two points for completing the aggressive option.
Two additional points are awarded for creating a scoring opportunity.
If the disposal turns over, the nearest player counterpresses.
Security players protect the corridor, deepest opponent and likely counterattack route.
The defending team receives three points for scoring from the turnover.
The attacking team receives one defensive point for stopping the counterattack before midfield.
Play remains live for up to 45 seconds.
Reset after a score, stoppage or completed recovery.
Rotate security and aggressive-running roles.
coachingPoints: High-risk transition requires preparation before the disposal.
Security players must identify the likely turnover location.
The nearest player to a failed disposal counterpresses immediately.
Other players protect the corridor and deepest threat.
Aggressive runners should not all move beyond the football.
The team should recognise when protection is insufficient to attempt the option.
Communication must identify the risk and defensive coverage.
A failed skill does not remove defensive responsibility.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether protection is established before the aggressive disposal.
Number and positioning of security players.
Whether the nearest player counterpresses.
Whether central and deep threats are protected.
Whether the team attempts risk without sufficient balance.
Whether players react emotionally to the turnover.
Whether the counterattack is delayed or stopped.

commonErrors.error: Every player runs ahead for the aggressive option.
commonErrors.correction: Retain connected security behind possession.

commonErrors.error: Security players react only after the turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Position according to the likely turnover route before the disposal.

commonErrors.error: The nearest player appeals or stops after an error.
commonErrors.correction: Counterpress immediately and delay the ball carrier.

commonErrors.error: Defenders chase wide opponents while the corridor is exposed.
commonErrors.correction: Protect central and deepest threats first.

commonErrors.error: Players attempt the high-risk option without support.
commonErrors.correction: Retain possession until adequate protection and connection exist.

progressions: Remove marked high-risk areas.
Add full match-like contact.
Introduce scoreboard scenarios requiring greater or lower risk.
Create numerical imbalance behind the football.
Continue into full-ground match simulation.
Use video to assess pre-turnover positioning.
regressions: Give the attacking team three security players.
successIndicators: Avoid aggressive options when balance is inadequate.
matchApplication: Aggressive transition can create scoring opportunities but also expose the team to damaging turnovers. Elite teams prepare for the possibility of failure before committing to the attacking action.

title: Repeated Turnover Scenario Ladder
primarySkill: Solving consecutive transition scenarios of increasing complexity.
objective: Develop the ability to repeatedly reset decision making as transition scenarios change in field position, pressure, numbers and match context.
groundSize: Full oval or a large field divided into defensive, midfield and forward scenario zones.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the ground into defensive, midfield and forward scenario zones.
Prepare a ladder of six scenarios:
Clean defensive regain
Pressured defensive regain
Midfield turnover with equal numbers
Midfield turnover while outnumbered
Forward-half regain
Late-game scoreboard transition
Divide players into two teams.
Place footballs at each scenario starting point.
Assign one coach or leader to trigger each next scenario immediately.
howTheDrillWorks:
Teams begin with Scenario 1 and play until the objective is completed or the football turns over.
The coach immediately initiates Scenario 2 without allowing full positional reset.
Players must recognise the new possession state, field position and numerical picture.
The ladder continues through all six scenarios.
Teams receive one point for completing each scenario objective.
A decision-quality point is awarded when the selected response suits the situation.
A communication point is awarded when players clearly identify the new scenario demands.
An avoidable turnover removes one point.
After completing the ladder, teams rest for two minutes.
Repeat with roles and scenario directions reversed.
Increase pressure or change the scoreboard context in later rounds.
Complete three to four total ladders.
coachingPoints: Players must mentally reset after every possession change.
The previous scenario’s solution may not suit the next one.
Communication should identify field position, numbers, pressure and time.
Defensive and attacking roles must reorganise without a coach-led pause.
Fatigue must not remove scanning and support.
Risk should increase or decrease according to the scenario.
Players must preserve behind-ball balance through the entire ladder.
Leaders should organise teammates without overcontrolling every decision.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Speed of mental and physical reset.
Whether players apply the previous solution inappropriately.
Recognition of changing field position.
Numerical and scoreboard awareness.
Communication quality.
Support and defensive balance under fatigue.
Whether decision quality declines later in the ladder.
Leadership and role clarity.

commonErrors.error: Players continue the previous scenario’s movement pattern.
commonErrors.correction: Reassess the full field before selecting the next action.

commonErrors.error: Communication becomes general and unclear.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the actual numbers, pressure and field position.

commonErrors.error: Later scenarios produce rushed decisions.
commonErrors.correction: Regain balance and scan despite fatigue.

commonErrors.error: Players wait for coach direction at each stage.
commonErrors.correction: Use player leaders to organise the next response.

commonErrors.error: Behind-ball protection disappears across the ladder.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain security responsibility through every phase.

progressions: Remove verbal scenario announcements.
Change the order of the ladder.
Add full match-like contact.
Alter scoreboard conditions during the sequence.
Introduce hidden numerical changes.
Record the ladder for team review.
successIndicators: Solve consecutive scenarios without coach dependence.
matchApplication: Matches contain repeated turnovers in different parts of the ground and under changing conditions. Players must solve each new transition phase rather than relying on the decision that worked moments earlier.

title: Advanced Transition Application Assessment
primarySkill: Integrating advanced transition manipulation, game management and risk control.
objective: Assess whether players can independently apply advanced transition decisions under changing pressure, numerical balance, fatigue and match context.
groundSize: Full oval.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use the full oval.
Divide players into two balanced teams with normal positional structure.
Prepare an assessment sheet covering:
Disguised release
Switch-trap recognition
Corridor manipulation
Scoreboard tempo
Decision making under fatigue
Numerical change recognition
Floating-player rotation
High-risk transition protection
Consecutive scenario adaptation
Defensive reaction after failed transition
Prepare several scoreboard and numerical scenarios.
Place spare footballs around the ground.
Use assistant coaches or leaders to observe different field zones.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play begins from a defensive regain and continues normally.
The coach periodically changes the scoreboard, time or numerical balance.
Defenders may use disguised pressure, delayed switch traps or corridor compression.
The attacking team must identify and manipulate the defensive structure.
One point is awarded for a controlled defensive exit.
One point is awarded for an appropriate tactical decision.
Two points are awarded for a line-breaking transition that retains protection behind the football.
Three points are awarded for a goal.
The opposition receives three points for scoring from an unprotected transition turnover.
Play four blocks of six minutes with one minute of feedback between blocks.
Increase fatigue and scenario complexity across the blocks.
Remove coach prompts and bonus scoring during the final block.
coachingPoints: Players must scan the whole field before committing to transition.
Tactical deception should influence defenders without delaying unnecessarily.
Apparent space may be a defensive trap.
Corridor movement can create outside space.
Score and time should alter transition tempo and risk.
Numerical balance must be reassessed continuously.
Floating or rotating players must not damage team security.
High-risk options require protection before the disposal.
Players must reset decisions after every turnover.
Behaviours must remain during the unrestricted final block.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players manipulate defensive movement.
Recognition of switch traps and false space.
Use of corridor threats to open width.
Adjustment to scoreboard and time.
Decision quality under fatigue.
Recognition of changing numbers.
Rotation around floating players.
Protection behind high-risk transition.
Adaptation through consecutive scenarios.
Communication and leadership.
Defensive reaction after errors.
Whether advanced behaviours remain without bonus scoring.

commonErrors.error: Players use deception without scanning the available field.
commonErrors.correction: Identify genuine options before attempting to manipulate defenders.

commonErrors.error: Teams move automatically towards visible space.
commonErrors.correction: Assess whether the space is open, supported or deliberately baited.

commonErrors.error: Scoreboard context does not alter transition tempo.
commonErrors.correction: Reconnect tactical risk to score and time.

commonErrors.error: Numerical changes are recognised too late.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate numbers immediately as players enter or recover.

commonErrors.error: High-risk movement leaves no security behind.
commonErrors.correction: Organise turnover protection before attempting the disposal.

commonErrors.error: Advanced behaviours disappear in unrestricted play.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce them as adaptable match principles rather than drill rules.

progressions: Use full match-like contact.
Allow the opposition to select its own pressing and trapping strategies.
Introduce unannounced scoreboard changes.
Create hidden numerical imbalances.
Use position-specific performance ratings.
Record the activity for detailed video review.
Continue into a full match-simulation block.
regressions: Reduce field length and player numbers.
Reduce running and contact demands for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Preserve decisions and skill under fatigue.
Reproduce advanced behaviours without bonus scoring.
matchApplication: This assessment measures whether players can apply advanced transition principles independently in conditions resembling senior and high-performance football. It tests manipulation, risk control, numerical awareness, fatigue resistance and match-context decision making before the chapter progresses into position-specific and full match-scenario work.

title: Defensive Unit Transition Roles
primarySkill: Executing position-specific defensive transition roles after gaining or losing possession.
objective: Develop clear transition responsibilities for key defenders, intercept defenders, running half-backs and deep defensive support players during both defence-to-attack and attack-to-defence phases.
groundSize: Defensive half of an oval, extending approximately 20 metres beyond defensive 50.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use defensive 50 and the space extending towards the wing and centre.
Divide players into a defensive unit and an opposition forward-pressure unit.
Within the defensive unit, identify:
Deep key defender
Intercept defender
Running half-backs
Small defenders
Behind-ball security player
Mark near-side, corridor and far-side exits.
Begin each repetition with a varied forward entry.
Rotate players through defensive roles across the activity.
howTheDrillWorks:
The opposition delivers the football inside 50.
The defensive unit attempts to intercept, spoil to advantage or win the ground ball.
The deepest defender protects goal-side space and the most dangerous forward.
The intercept defender reads the entry and attacks the aerial or loose football.
Running half-backs spread to create near-side and far-side outlets.
Small defenders secure front-and-centre and ground-level threats.
Once possession is won, the unit attempts to complete three connected disposals and exit defensive 50.
If possession is lost during the exit, the nearest defender pressures while others protect the corridor and deepest threat.
The defensive unit receives one point for securing the regain and two points for a controlled exit.
The forward unit receives three points for scoring from a transition turnover.
Reset after a score, successful exit, stoppage or 40 seconds.
Review one positional role after every three repetitions.
coachingPoints: Each defender’s transition response depends on starting position and role.
The deepest defender should not abandon goal-side security to chase the football.
Intercept defenders must attack the ball while teammates cover behind them.
Running defenders should create width as possession becomes secure.
Small defenders must protect the dangerous ground-level space.
The first disposal should reduce pressure rather than transfer it.
Defensive roles must reorganise immediately if the exit turns over.
Communication should identify intercept, cover, outlet and deepest responsibilities.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defensive roles remain clear before the regain.
Whether the deepest defender protects dangerous space.
Whether the intercept defender receives support behind.
Whether running half-backs spread early.
Whether small defenders position front-and-centre.
Quality of the first disposal.
Whether defenders reconnect after exiting.
Reaction when possession turns over again.

commonErrors.error: Every defender attacks the same aerial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Keep one defender deepest and assign ground-level coverage.

commonErrors.error: The deepest defender runs forward before possession is secure.
commonErrors.correction: Hold goal-side security until the exit is established.

commonErrors.error: Half-backs remain close to the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Spread early and create visible outlets.

commonErrors.error: The intercept defender attacks without cover behind.
commonErrors.correction: Complete the defensive handover before leaving position.

commonErrors.error: Defenders stop after the first disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Continue supporting until the football exits defensive pressure.

progressions: Remove the marked role positions.
Add full match-like forward pressure.
Start from repeated inside-50 entries.
Continue play to the opposite forward line.
Introduce scoreboard and time scenarios.
Allow the opposition to alter its forward structure between repetitions.
regressions: Give the defensive unit an extra player.
Stop after the defensive regain to establish roles.
Reduce running distances for Over 35 players.
matchApplication: Effective defensive transition requires more than every player reacting towards the football. Key defenders, interceptors, small defenders and running half-backs must perform complementary roles that secure the regain and begin attack without exposing goal-side space.

title: Midfield Unit Transition Roles
primarySkill: Executing position-specific midfield transition responsibilities.
objective: Develop coordinated transition roles for inside midfielders, outside midfielders and defensive midfield support during repeated possession changes.
groundSize: Central 80 metres of the ground, including the centre square and both half-back and half-forward areas.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a central playing area extending from half-back to half-forward.
Place a scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two midfield units.
Within each unit, identify:
Inside ball winner
Defensive midfielder
Forward-running midfielder
Outside midfielder
Underneath support midfielder
Begin from stoppages, loose footballs and coach-created turnovers.
Rotate roles every four repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play begins with a midfield contest or controlled possession.
When a team gains possession, the inside ball winner secures and releases the football.
The outside midfielder provides width.
The forward-running midfielder moves ahead into attacking connection.
The underneath midfielder supports behind the football.
When possession is lost, the nearest midfielder pressures.
The defensive midfielder protects the corridor and tracks the most dangerous runner.
Other midfielders recover goal-side and reconnect with defenders.
The attacking team receives one point for exiting the contest and two points for reaching its scoring gate.
The defending team receives one point for forcing a backwards disposal and three for regaining possession.
Play continues through repeated turnovers for up to 45 seconds.
Reset and review role execution after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Inside midfielders must secure possession before releasing.
Outside midfielders should preserve width rather than entering every contest.
One midfielder should support underneath the football.
Forward runners must time movement to possession security.
The nearest player pressures after a turnover.
Defensive midfielders protect the corridor and dangerous runners.
Midfielders must work in both directions rather than specialising in one phase.
Communication should identify inside, outside, hold, recover and deepest roles.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether midfielders maintain role diversity.
Security of the first possession.
Outside width during the transition.
Timing of forward-running midfielders.
Availability of underneath support.
Corridor protection after turnovers.
Defensive tracking effort.
Whether role clarity remains under fatigue.

commonErrors.error: Every midfielder attacks the initial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Hold one outside player and one underneath support player.

commonErrors.error: Forward runners leave before possession is secure.
commonErrors.correction: Time the run to the ball winner’s control.

commonErrors.error: No midfielder supports behind the football.
commonErrors.correction: Assign an underneath connection and security role.

commonErrors.error: Midfielders chase direct opponents into wide space.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the corridor and most dangerous runner first.

commonErrors.error: Players perform only attacking or defensive work.
commonErrors.correction: Rotate roles and score two-way transition actions.

progressions: Remove marked midfield roles.
Add full match-like stoppage contact.
Introduce changing numerical balance.
Continue from midfield into full forward entries.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Require role handovers during the same phase.
regressions: Give the possession team a neutral midfielder.
Shorten repeated running for Over 35 players.
matchApplication: Midfielders are central to transition because they influence both the initial contest and the connection between defence and attack. Effective midfield units maintain role balance rather than sending every player towards the same action.

title: Wing Transition Roles
primarySkill: Executing wing-specific attacking and defensive transition roles.
objective: Develop wing players’ ability to provide attacking width, switch connection and defensive corridor support according to ball location and possession state.
groundSize: Approximately 80 metres long × 60 metres wide, using both wings and the corridor.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a near-side wing, corridor and far-side wing.
Place one scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams.
Assign one wing player to each side for both teams.
Position other players through half-back, midfield and half-forward.
Begin from defensive and midfield regains on alternating sides.
Rotate wing players every four repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team gains possession near a boundary or through the corridor.
The near-side wing provides an immediate outside or forward option.
The far-side wing holds width and prepares for a switch.
If the team loses possession, the near-side wing pressures or tracks the outside outlet.
The far-side wing folds towards the corridor while preserving far-side awareness.
When possession changes again, both wings expand quickly.
One point is awarded for effective near-side support.
One point is awarded for maintaining usable far-side width.
Two points are awarded for a successful switch through a wing.
The defending team receives two points when a wing’s recovery closes a dangerous lane.
Play continues through repeated turnovers for 40 seconds.
Reset and alternate the starting side.
coachingPoints: Near-side and far-side wing roles differ.
The near-side wing should support the immediate possession phase.
The far-side wing must maintain width without becoming disconnected.
After losing possession, wings should fold enough to protect the corridor.
Wings must scan inside and behind, not only follow the boundary.
Far-side width can become the best attacking option after a regain.
Wing players should preserve the ability to move in both directions.
Communication should identify switch, fold, hold and inside support.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Position of near-side and far-side wings.
Whether far-side width remains usable.
Whether wings fold appropriately in defence.
Timing of switch movement.
Whether wing receivers have inside support.
Whether players become trapped against the boundary.
Two-way running effort.
Role adjustment after repeated turnovers.

commonErrors.error: Both wings move to the same side of the ground.
commonErrors.correction: Preserve far-side width and team balance.

commonErrors.error: The far-side wing remains too wide after possession is lost.
commonErrors.correction: Fold towards the corridor while tracking the switch threat.

commonErrors.error: The near-side wing stands flat-footed.
commonErrors.correction: Lead into space and provide a moving outlet.

commonErrors.error: Wings receive without inside support.
commonErrors.correction: Connect a midfielder or half-back beneath the wing.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after a switch disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Continue supporting the next forward action.

progressions: Remove wing-lane markers.
Add full match-like pressure.
Require wing players to rotate with half-backs and half-forwards.
Continue into a full forward-entry phase.
Introduce hidden switch traps.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
regressions: Stop after each turnover to review wing positioning.
Reduce repeated running for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Execute different near-side and far-side roles.
matchApplication: Wing players provide critical balance during transition. Their positioning determines whether the team can access width in attack while still protecting the corridor and opposite-side movement in defence.
relatedDrills: TR-063 – Wing Release and Inside Support

title: Forward Unit Transition Roles
primarySkill: Executing forward-specific transition roles after gaining or losing possession.
objective: Develop clear transition roles for deep forwards, high forwards and pressure forwards during forward entries, defensive exits and forward-half regains.
groundSize: Forward half of an oval, including forward 50 and high half-forward space.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use one forward half.
Divide players into a forward unit and defensive unit.
Within the forward unit, identify:
Deep forward
High forward
Pressure forwards
Forward-half security player
Mark near-side, corridor and far-side defensive exits.
Begin each repetition with a forward entry.
Vary whether the entry is marked, spoiled, intercepted or won at ground level.
howTheDrillWorks:
The forward unit organises leads and support during the entry.
If the forward team wins possession, it attempts to create a controlled scoring opportunity.
If the defensive team regains possession, forward roles immediately change.
The nearest pressure forward closes the ball carrier.
Other pressure forwards deny the short and corridor exits.
The high forward protects the next release or midfield connection.
The deep forward either pressures locally or protects the dangerous switch route according to position.
If the forward team regains possession, players spread into direct, wide and underneath scoring options.
The forward unit receives three points for a goal and two points for a repeat entry.
The defensive unit receives three points for a controlled exit.
Play continues for up to 40 seconds.
Reset and rotate forward roles.
coachingPoints: Forward transition begins immediately when an entry is lost.
The nearest forward pressures while others close exits.
High forwards must protect the connection beyond defensive 50.
Deep forwards should avoid chasing harmless possession away from goal.
Forward-half regains should be secured before a rushed shot.
Players must create varied scoring options after regaining possession.
At least one player should remain behind the attacking contest.
Communication should identify pressure, corridor, switch and deepest roles.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Reaction after a lost forward entry.
Nearest-player pressure.
Coverage of corridor and short exits.
High-forward positioning.
Whether deep forwards chase unnecessarily.
Quality of forward-half regains.
Organisation of scoring options.
Security behind the attacking contest.

commonErrors.error: Every forward chases the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Assign pressure, outlet-denial and deeper-cover roles.

commonErrors.error: The high forward moves too deep into the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Hold position to protect the next defensive exit.

commonErrors.error: Deep forwards stop after an intercepted entry.
commonErrors.correction: Pressure locally or protect the dangerous route.

commonErrors.error: Forward-half regains produce rushed shots.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession and improve the scoring opportunity.

commonErrors.error: No player remains behind the attacking contest.
commonErrors.correction: Retain forward-half security against another turnover.

progressions: Add full match-like defensive pressure.
Remove the marked defensive exits.
Introduce different defensive exit systems.
Continue play to the opposite end after a successful exit.
Add scoreboard and late-game scenarios.
Allow forward players to rotate roles during the same phase.
regressions: Give the forward unit a numerical advantage.
Begin with a controlled forward-half regain.
Reduce repeat efforts for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: React immediately after losing an entry.
Apply pressure through the nearest forward.
matchApplication: Forwards influence transition both by creating scoring options and by preventing defensive exits. Clear forward roles help generate repeat entries without exposing the team to easy counterattack.

title: Ruck and Stoppage Transition Roles
primarySkill: Executing ruck and stoppage-specific transition responsibilities.
objective: Develop coordinated transition roles for rucks, inside midfielders and outside stoppage players immediately after the stoppage outcome becomes clear.
groundSize: A 25-metre stoppage area inside a 65-metre × 45-metre transition field.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a central stoppage circle or throw-in area.
Place a scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two stoppage units.
Within each unit, identify:
Ruck
First-possession midfielder
Defensive midfielder
Outside midfielder
High support player
Begin from ball-ups, boundary throw-ins and ground-ball stoppage simulations.
Rotate roles across several starts.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins the stoppage.
The rucks compete and follow the football after the hit-out.
Inside midfielders attempt to secure the first possession.
Outside players hold shape until the football’s direction becomes clear.
The team winning possession releases outside or forward.
The team losing possession pressures the clearance source.
The defensive midfielder protects the corridor and tracks the first forward runner.
The ruck either supports the clearance or folds behind the football.
One point is awarded for winning the first possession.
Two points are awarded for exiting the stoppage area under control.
Two additional points are awarded for reaching a scoring gate.
Reset after a score, turnover, secondary stoppage or 35 seconds.
coachingPoints: Rucks must transition after the hit-out rather than watching the outcome.
Inside midfielders should secure possession before forcing clearance.
Outside players must hold width and avoid collapsing early.
The team losing possession should pressure the source immediately.
Defensive midfielders protect the corridor and dangerous runners.
The ruck can become a support or defensive security player.
Players must react to the actual hit-out rather than the planned one.
Communication should identify possession, pressure, outside and recovery roles.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Ruck follow-up effort.
Security of the first possession.
Outside positioning.
Quality of the stoppage release.
Immediate clearance pressure.
Defensive midfield positioning.
Ruck support behind or beside the football.
Reaction to unexpected hit-out outcomes.

commonErrors.error: The ruck stops after the tap.
commonErrors.correction: Follow the football and become support or pressure.

commonErrors.error: Outside midfielders collapse into the stoppage.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width until possession direction is clear.

commonErrors.error: The clearance player kicks blindly.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession and use an outside or supported release.

commonErrors.error: Defensive midfielders chase the football.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the corridor and dangerous forward runner.

commonErrors.error: Players move according to the planned hit rather than the actual outcome.
commonErrors.correction: Read the live football and adjust immediately.

progressions: Add full match-like stoppage contact.
Remove fixed stoppage roles.
Introduce numerical imbalance outside the contest.
Continue into full-ground play.
Add scoreboard and late-game stoppage scenarios.
Run consecutive stoppages without positional reset.
regressions: Give one team an extra outside player.
Reduce repeat efforts for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Follow the hit-out with a second action.
Use the ruck as support or security.
Transition from stoppage into open play.
matchApplication: Stoppages create immediate transition moments once possession becomes clear. Rucks and midfielders must move from set stoppage roles into open-play attack or defence without hesitation.

title: Kick-In to Open-Play Transition
primarySkill: Moving from a kick-in structure into open-play transition.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to launch from a kick-in, connect beyond defensive 50 and adapt when the planned exit becomes live open play.
groundSize: Defensive two-thirds of an oval.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use the goal square, defensive 50 and middle third.
Position one team in a kick-in structure.
Position the opposition in a zone, press or player-to-player structure.
Mark near-side, corridor and far-side exits beyond defensive 50.
Place target players through the middle third.
Prepare several opposition pressing structures.
Rotate kickers and primary outlet players.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play begins with a kick-in.
The kicker scans the opposition structure and selects an initial exit.
Defenders and midfielders move to create width, depth and switch support.
Once the first possession is completed, all kick-in restrictions end and play becomes live.
The team attempts to connect beyond defensive 50 and through the middle third.
If the planned option closes, the team uses a reset, switch or controlled contest.
One point is awarded for completing the first kick-in possession.
One point is awarded for exiting defensive 50.
Two points are awarded for controlled middle-third possession.
The opposition receives three points for scoring from a kick-in turnover.
Play continues for up to 45 seconds.
Reset from another kick-in using a different defensive press.
coachingPoints: The kick-in is the beginning of transition, not a separate isolated play.
Players should respond to the actual opposition structure.
The first receiver must have support for the next action.
Far-side options should remain available.
Players must not become fixed to the planned kick-in pattern.
Behind-ball security remains essential during the exit.
The kicker may become a supporting player after disposal.
The team must react defensively immediately if the kick-in turns over.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
The kicker’s scanning and decision.
Timing of outlet movement.
Support around the first receiver.
Whether players remain fixed to a rehearsed pattern.
Far-side and reset availability.
Connection into the middle third.
Positioning behind the football.
Defensive reaction after a turnover.

commonErrors.error: Players run predetermined routes despite opposition coverage.
commonErrors.correction: Read the live press and adapt the exit.

commonErrors.error: The first receiver is isolated.
commonErrors.correction: Build second and third actions around the initial kick.

commonErrors.error: Far-side players move towards the first option.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width and maintain switch potential.

commonErrors.error: The kicker stops after disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Become support behind or beside the football.

commonErrors.error: Players relax after exiting defensive 50.
commonErrors.correction: Continue transition through the middle third.

progressions: Remove all exit markers.
Add full match-like pressure.
Allow the opposition to change its press during the kick-in.
Continue to a full-ground scoring phase.
Introduce scoreboard and time scenarios.
Require players to identify the opposition structure before restarting.
regressions: Give the kick-in team an extra outlet player.
Reduce field length for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Adapt when the planned route closes.
matchApplication: A kick-in quickly becomes an open-play transition once the first possession is completed. Successful teams connect their starting structure to the next several actions rather than judging success only by the first kick.
relatedDrills: TR-009 – First Exit After Defensive Regain

title: Full-Ground Turnover Zones
primarySkill: Adjusting transition behaviour according to turnover location.
objective: Develop distinct team transition responses for turnovers occurring in defensive 50, the defensive midfield area, the corridor, the wing and the forward half.
groundSize: Full oval.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the oval into five turnover reference zones:
Defensive 50
Defensive midfield
Central corridor
Wing
Forward half
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Position players in normal match structure.
Place footballs with coaches in each zone.
Establish a broad preferred response for each location without creating fixed patterns.
Use assistant coaches or player leaders to observe separate zones.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play begins normally from one end.
The coach creates or identifies a turnover in one of the five zones.
Players must recognise the turnover location and execute an appropriate response.
Defensive 50 regains prioritise security and exit.
Midfield regains assess fast attack, switch or possession control.
Corridor turnovers trigger immediate counterpressing or central recovery.
Wing turnovers require boundary awareness and inside support.
Forward-half regains prioritise organised scoring and repeat pressure.
One decision-quality point is awarded for using an appropriate zone response.
Normal scoring applies for goals and behinds.
Play continues through several turnovers before resetting.
Complete four blocks, each emphasising different turnover locations.
coachingPoints: Turnover location changes both opportunity and risk.
Defensive 50 requires possession security.
Central turnovers demand immediate pressure and corridor protection.
Wing turnovers require awareness of boundary and inside support.
Forward-half regains should create controlled scoring opportunities.
Players must not use the same solution everywhere.
Communication should identify the turnover zone and required action.
Team lines should adjust together rather than as isolated players.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Recognition of turnover location.
Whether response matches the zone.
Security of defensive regains.
Counterpressing after central turnovers.
Use of boundary and inside options on the wing.
Organisation after forward-half regains.
Communication across positional lines.
Whether players revert to one habitual solution.

commonErrors.error: Players attack at the same speed from every zone.
commonErrors.correction: Match transition tempo to field position and risk.

commonErrors.error: Defensive 50 regains are treated like midfield turnovers.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession and complete the exit first.

commonErrors.error: Central turnovers create individual chasing.
commonErrors.correction: Apply coordinated pressure with protection behind.

commonErrors.error: Wing turnovers become trapped against the boundary.
commonErrors.correction: Provide inside and trailing support.

commonErrors.error: Forward-half regains produce immediate low-quality shots.
commonErrors.correction: Organise the possession and improve the scoring opportunity.

progressions: Remove visible zone markers.
Allow full match-like pressure.
Create consecutive turnovers in different zones.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Give each team different tactical preferences.
Record and review zone decisions.
matchApplication: The correct transition response depends heavily on where possession changes. A decision that is appropriate in the forward half may be unnecessarily risky inside defensive 50.

title: Momentum and Red-Time Transition
primarySkill: Managing transition during momentum swings and the final minutes of a quarter.
objective: Develop team responses for controlling or changing match momentum and managing transition during red-time periods late in quarters.
groundSize: Full oval.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use the full oval.
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Prepare momentum and red-time scenarios such as:
Opposition has kicked three consecutive goals.
Team has kicked three consecutive goals.
Two minutes remain in the quarter with scores level.
Team leads by eight points with 90 seconds remaining.
Team trails by ten points with two minutes remaining.
Begin each scenario from a varied turnover or stoppage.
Assign player leaders responsibility for communicating score and time.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach announces the scenario.
Play begins from the designated field position.
Players select transition tempo, route and risk according to momentum, score and time.
A team under opposition momentum may prioritise possession, territory and defensive structure.
A team with momentum may attack while preserving security behind the football.
Red-time scenarios require repeated communication of remaining time.
Normal match scoring applies.
A decision-quality point is awarded for an appropriate transition response.
A preventable central turnover during a protection scenario gives the opposition a bonus point.
Each scenario runs for one to three minutes.
Teams reverse the match situation and repeat.
Finish with an unannounced scenario players must identify from the scoreboard.
coachingPoints: Momentum affects emotional state but should not remove tactical discipline.
Teams under pressure may need to slow the game and complete possession.
Teams with momentum should not abandon turnover protection.
Red-time transition requires awareness of score, time and field position.
Players should communicate the clock regularly.
Boundary and territory can be valuable late in quarters.
When trailing, urgency should still produce organised scoring opportunities.
The team must understand when a stoppage is a positive outcome.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players understand the match situation.
Transition tempo under momentum pressure.
Risk selection late in quarters.
Communication of score and time.
Use of boundary and territory.
Protection behind attacking movement.
Emotional response after opposition scores.
Whether the team can change tempo deliberately.

commonErrors.error: Players rush after conceding several goals.
commonErrors.correction: Complete possession and restore team structure before attacking.

commonErrors.error: A team with momentum sends every player forward.
commonErrors.correction: Preserve behind-ball protection against counterattack.

commonErrors.error: Players forget the clock.
commonErrors.correction: Assign leaders to communicate remaining time repeatedly.

commonErrors.error: A leading team attacks through unnecessary central risk.
commonErrors.correction: Use safer possession, boundary and territory options.

commonErrors.error: A trailing team becomes reckless.
commonErrors.correction: Create urgency through movement and support rather than blind disposal.

progressions: Change the score during the scenario.
Hide the clock from selected players.
Allow full match-like contact.
Introduce opposition time-wasting or aggressive pressing strategies.
Run consecutive red-time phases without rest.
Record communication and decisions for review.
regressions: Stop halfway to review the scoreboard.
Provide the preferred strategy before starting.
successIndicators: Use possession, boundary and territory effectively.
matchApplication: Late-quarter transition and momentum periods often decide matches. Teams must manage emotion, tempo, territory and risk rather than playing every possession at the same speed.

title: Match Scenario Transition Simulation
primarySkill: Applying complete transition systems across realistic match scenarios.
objective: Prepare players for the final chapter assessment by integrating position-specific roles, turnover-zone responses, match context and full-ground transition under realistic pressure.
groundSize: Full oval.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use the full oval.
Divide players into two balanced match teams.
Establish normal positional structures.
Prepare six scenarios:
Defensive 50 regain against a high press
Midfield turnover with numerical advantage
Midfield turnover while outnumbered
Forward-half regain
Kick-in transition
Red-time scoreboard transition
Assign coaching observers to defence, midfield, wings and forwards.
Player leaders manage communication and structure.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins Scenario 1 and allows play to continue until the objective is completed or possession stabilises.
The next scenario starts immediately from a different field position.
Players must reorganise without a complete positional reset.
Position groups execute their transition responsibilities.
Normal match scoring applies.
One team-structure point is awarded for maintaining line connection.
One decision-quality point is awarded for selecting an appropriate transition response.
One defensive point is awarded for organised pressure and recovery after losing possession.
An avoidable turnover caused by poor transition balance removes one point.
Complete the six-scenario sequence twice.
On the second sequence, alter opposition tactics and scoreboard conditions.
Finish with five minutes of unrestricted play.
coachingPoints: Position-specific roles must support the whole-team response.
Players should recognise field position before selecting transition speed.
Numerical advantage should be used before it disappears.
Numerical disadvantage should be managed through security and delay.
Defensive 50 regains require calm exit connection.
Forward-half regains require organised scoring and pressure.
Kick-in structure must flow into open play.
Red-time scenarios alter risk and tempo.
Leadership communication should organise without removing player decision making.
Transition behaviours must remain during unrestricted play.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Defensive-unit role execution.
Midfield balance and two-way running.
Wing width and defensive folding.
Forward pressure and scoring organisation.
Stoppage and kick-in transition.
Recognition of numerical balance.
Scoreboard and time management.
Communication between positional lines.
Behind-ball security.
Adaptation when opposition tactics change.
Recovery after failed transition.
Behaviour during unrestricted play.

commonErrors.error: Position groups perform their roles without connecting to teammates.
commonErrors.correction: Judge every role by its effect on the complete team structure.

commonErrors.error: Players wait for a full reset between scenarios.
commonErrors.correction: Reorganise immediately from the current field position.

commonErrors.error: The same transition route is used repeatedly.
commonErrors.correction: Read pressure, field position and available numbers.

commonErrors.error: Leaders give constant instructions that slow decisions.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate essential information and allow teammates to act.

commonErrors.error: Structure disappears during unrestricted play.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce the same principles without drill scoring or coach prompts.

progressions: Allow opposition teams to create their own scenarios.
Remove all coach announcements.
Increase match-like contact.
Add quarter-length scoreboard simulation.
Use video and GPS data where available.
Include special situations such as a player off the ground or deliberate defensive spare.
regressions: Shorten the simulation for Over 35 players.
matchApplication: This simulation combines the position-specific, tactical and contextual demands of transition. It tests whether the team can move between different match situations without relying on complete resets or constant coach direction.

title: Transition Chapter Final Assessment
primarySkill: Demonstrating complete individual, positional and team transition capability.
objective: Complete the final assessment of the Transition chapter by evaluating whether players and the team can independently recognise, organise and execute all major transition behaviours under full match conditions.
groundSize: Full oval.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use the full oval.
Divide players into two balanced match teams.
Use normal positional structures and rotations.
Assign observers to assess:
Individual transition reaction
Defensive unit
Midfield unit
Wings
Forward unit
Whole-team shape
Match-context decision making
Prepare assessment categories covering the full chapter:
Turnover recognition
First-three-second response
Immediate pressure
Corridor recovery
First-possession security
Attacking spread
Support running
Defensive exit
Team line connection
Position-specific roles
Numerical decision making
Scoreboard management
Turnover protection
Communication and leadership
Begin with normal match conditions rather than a predetermined pattern.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play begins as a full match simulation.
Coaches allow natural turnovers to occur without immediate intervention.
During the first block, no bonus points or coach prompts are used.
During the second block, the coach introduces selected scenarios including:
Defensive 50 regain
Central turnover
Forward-half regain
Stoppage spill
Kick-in
Numerical imbalance
Red-time scoreboard situation
Normal match scoring applies throughout.
Individual players are assessed on recognition, effort, role execution and decision quality.
Position groups are assessed on connection and role clarity.
The whole team is assessed on shape change, route selection and turnover protection.
Play four blocks of eight to ten minutes.
Give only brief principle-based feedback between blocks.
Complete the final block without coach-created scenarios or transition scoring.
Conduct a post-session review using observations, player feedback and video where available.
coachingPoints: Players must recognise turnovers independently.
The first three seconds should contain purposeful attacking or defensive action.
Nearest-player pressure must be supported by cover and balance.
Defensive recovery should protect corridor, goal-side and deepest space.
Regains must be secured through the first and second possessions.
The attacking team should create width, depth and connected support.
Defensive exits require composure and several linked actions.
Team lines must move together through full-ground transition.
Position-specific responsibilities must contribute to the complete team shape.
Numerical advantage and disadvantage must be recognised quickly.
Scoreboard, time and field position should influence risk.
High-risk transition requires protection behind the football.
Communication must be early, specific and useful.
Transition behaviours should remain without external scoring or coach prompts.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Speed of turnover recognition.
Quality of first actions.
Nearest-player pressure.
Corridor and goal-side recovery.
Security of the first two possessions.
Attacking width, depth and support.
Quality of defensive exits.
Connection between defenders, midfielders, wings and forwards.
Position-specific transition roles.
Numerical awareness.
Match-context decision making.
Protection behind high-risk transition.
Communication and leadership.
Repeat effort under fatigue.
Adaptation to opposition tactics.
Behaviour during unrestricted match simulation.

commonErrors.error: Players recognise turnovers only after teammates react.
commonErrors.correction: Scan continuously and take independent responsibility for the first action.

commonErrors.error: Pressure is applied without support behind it.
commonErrors.correction: Establish cover, corridor protection and deeper balance.

commonErrors.error: The team wins possession but loses the next disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Secure the first and second possessions before expanding fully.

commonErrors.error: Position groups become disconnected.
commonErrors.correction: Move the entire team shape with the football.

commonErrors.error: Players use the same transition response in every location.
commonErrors.correction: Match the action to field position, pressure, numbers and scoreboard.

commonErrors.error: Aggressive transition leaves no protection behind.
commonErrors.correction: Organise security before attempting high-risk movement.

commonErrors.error: Communication disappears under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain clear role and pressure calls throughout the session.

commonErrors.error: Behaviours appear only during coach-created scenarios.
commonErrors.correction: Assess and reinforce transition habits during unrestricted play.

progressions: Extend into full quarter-length match simulation.
Use full senior match contact where appropriate.
Allow teams to design and alter their own transition systems.
Include opposition tactical changes between quarters.
Add player-number scenarios such as rotations, injuries or temporary imbalance.
Use detailed video coding and statistical transition review.
Establish individual and positional development plans from assessment results.
regressions: Assess one half of the ground at a time.
Reduce player numbers and field dimensions.
Evaluate selected transition categories rather than the full chapter.
Pause after major turnovers to review shape.
Shorten blocks and running distances for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Apply organised pressure and defensive recovery.
Secure the first and second possessions.
Create attacking width, depth and support.
Sustain repeat effort and decision quality.
Reproduce transition behaviours during unrestricted match play.
matchApplication: This final assessment represents the complete Transition chapter. It determines whether players can independently move from attack to defence and defence to attack across contests, field positions, positional roles, tactical systems and match scenarios. Successful performance indicates that transition principles have become repeatable team behaviours rather than isolated drill actions.
relatedDrills: TR-070 – Team Ball Movement Transition Assessment
